عجزنا في بعض هذه الأسامي المتقاربة عن هذين المسلكين فينبغي أن نعتقد
تفاوتا بين معنى اللفظين وإن عجزنا عن التنصيص على خصوص ما به الافتراق
كالعظيم والكبير مثلا فإنه يصعب علينا أن نذكر وجه الفرق بين معنييهما في
حق  الله تعالى ولكنا لا نشك في أصل الافتراق
ولذلك قال عز من قائل الكبرياء ردائي والعظمة إزاري ففرق بينهما فرقا يدل
على التفاوت فإن كل واحد من الرداء والإزار زينة للابس ولكن الرداء أشرف من
الإزار
ولذلك جعل مفتاح الصلاة الله أكبر ولم يقم عند ذوي البصائر النافذة الله
أعلم مقامه وكذلك العرب في استعمالها تفرق بين اللفظين إذ تستعمل الكبير
حيث لا تستعمل العظيم ولو كانا مترادفين لتواردا في كل
مقام تقول العرب فلان أكبر سنا من فلان ولا تقول أعظم سنا وكذلك الجليل
غير الكبير والعظيم فإن الجلال يشير إلى صفات الشرف ولذلك لا يقال فلان أجل
سنا من فلان ويقال أكبر ويقال العرش أعظم من الإنسان ولا يقال أجل من
الإنسان
فهذه الأسامي وإن كانت متقاربة المعاني فليست مترادفة وعلى الجملة يبعد
الترادف المحض في الأسماء الداخلة في التسعة والتسعين لأن الأسامي لا تراد
لحروفها ومخارج أصواتها بل لمفهوماتها ومعانيها فهذا أصل لا بد من اعتقاده
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ك-ب-ر (k-b-r) and ع-ظ-م (ʿ-ẓ-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: كبر denotes magnitude in size, rank, or age; عظم denotes physical or moral grandeur, thickness, and elevation of status.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): الكبرياء is an exclusive divine attribute signifying His majesty that admits no rival; العظمة denotes His sublimity that overwhelms all comprehension.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Both are used literally of God, but in created contexts they diverge — one says أَكْبَرُ سِنًّا (older in age) but not أَعْظَمُ سِنًّا, proving non-synonymy.
- Root: غ-ف-ر (gh-f-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: غفر means to cover, conceal, and pardon; the intensive forms غفور and غفار intensify the act.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): المغفرة is the divine covering of sins; الغفور denotes abundant forgiveness relative to abundant sins; الغفار denotes repeated forgiveness, time after time.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The distinction is literal (ḥaqīqah) — each form carries a distinct quantitative or repetitive nuance, not mere rhetorical variation.
- Sībawayh Rule: Intensification and Incremental Meaning (al-mubālaghah wa ziyādat al-maʿnā) — The morphological patterns (wazn) faʿūl and faʿʿāl in Arabic grammar systematically add semantic increments (multiplicity, repetition) beyond the base form faʿil, entailing that such forms cannot be pure synonyms.
chapters.translation:
I say: Those who have delved into the explanation of these Names have not addressed this matter, nor have they deemed it improbable that two names might denote only a single meaning — such as al-Kabīr (the Great) and al-ʿAẓīm (the Magnificent), al-Qādir (the Powerful) and al-Muqtadir (the Omnipotent), and al-Khāliq (the Creator), al-Bāriʾ (the Originator), and al-Muṣawwir (the Fashioner). This, however, is something I deem utterly improbable — utmost improbability — whenever the two names belong to the ninety-nine. For a name is not intended for its letters, but rather for its meanings. Synonyms differ only in their letters. The excellence of these Names lies precisely in the meanings they bear. If they were emptied of meaning, nothing would remain but mere utterances. And a meaning, if indicated by a thousand names, would have no excellence over a meaning indicated by a single name. It is therefore improbable that this limited, enumerated number should be completed by repeating mere words over a single meaning. Rather, the more fitting view is that beneath every word there lies a specific meaning.

Thus, when we encounter two words that are close [in meaning], one of two things is necessarily entailed:

The first is that it becomes evident that one of them falls outside the ninety-nine — such as al-Aḥad (the One) and al-Wāḥid (the Unique). For in the well-known narration from Abū Hurayrah (may God be pleased with him), al-Wāḥid occurs, while in another narration al-Aḥad occurs in its place. Thus the number is completed with the meaning of divine unity (al-tawḥīd), whether expressed by the word al-Wāḥid or by the word al-Aḥad. But that the two should stand in completing the number as two names while their meaning is one — this is, to me, extremely remote.

The second is that we take pains to demonstrate a distinctive merit of one word over the other, by showing that it contains an indication that the other does not convey. An example: if al-Ghāfir (the Forgiver), al-Ghafūr (the Much-Forgiving), and al-Ghaffār (the Repeatedly-Forgiving) were all transmitted, it would not be improbable to count these as three Names. For al-Ghāfir indicates only the root act of forgiveness (aṣl al-maghfirah); al-Ghafūr indicates abundance of forgiveness relative to abundance of sins — so much so that one who forgives only a single type of sin might not be called al-Ghafūr; and al-Ghaffār points to abundance in the mode of repetition — that is, forgiving sins time after time — so much so that one who forgives all sins but only the first time, and does not forgive the one who returns to sin repeatedly, does not merit the name al-Ghaffār.

Likewise, al-Ghanī (the Self-Sufficient) and al-Malik (the Sovereign). For al-Ghanī is the one who has no need of anything; and al-Malik is also the one who has no need of anything, yet everything has need of him. Thus al-Malik conveys the meaning of al-Ghanī plus an addition. Similarly, al-ʿAlīm (the Knowing) and al-Khabīr (the All-Aware): al-ʿAlīm indicates knowledge alone, while al-Khabīr indicates His knowledge of inward, hidden matters. This measure of differentiation removes these Names from being synonyms, and places them in the class of "sword" (sayf), "Indian blade" (muhannad), and "sharp-cutting" (ṣārim) — not in the class of "lion" (asad) and "lion" (layth).

If, however, we are unable in the case of some of these close-meaning Names to pursue either of these two paths, then we ought to affirm a differentiation between the meanings of the two words, even if we are unable to specify precisely the particular point of divergence — as with al-ʿAẓīm and al-Kabīr, for example. For it is difficult for us to state the aspect of difference between their two meanings with respect to God (may He be exalted), yet we do not doubt the fact of their divergence.

For this reason, the Mighty and Majestic said: «الكبرياء ردائي والعظمة إزاري» — "Pride is My cloak and Grandeur is My lower garment" — and He distinguished between them with a distinction that indicates differentiation. For each of the cloak (ridāʾ) and the lower garment (izār) is an adornment for the wearer, but the cloak is nobler than the lower garment.

For this same reason, He made the key to prayer "Allāhu Akbar" (God is Greater), and among those of penetrating insight, "Allāhu Aʿlam" (God is Most Knowing) would not stand in its place. Likewise, the Arabs in their usage distinguish between the two words, employing kabīr where they would not employ ʿaẓīm. Were the two synonyms, they would be used interchangeably in every context. The Arabs say: "So-and-so is akbar (older) in age than so-and-so," but they do not say "aʿẓam in age." Similarly, al-Jalīl (the Majestic) is other than al-Kabīr and al-ʿAẓīm, for al-Jalāl points to attributes of honor and nobility. For this reason, one does not say "So-and-so is ajall in age than so-and-so," but rather "akbar." And one says "the Throne is aʿẓam (greater) than man," but not "ajall than man."

These Names, then, even though their meanings are close, are not synonyms. In sum, pure synonymy (al-tarāduf al-maḥḍ) is improbable among the Names entering into the ninety-nine, because Names are not intended for their letters and the articulations of their sounds, but rather for their conceptual contents and meanings. This, then, is a principle that must be affirmed.

chapters.title_en: Section 4 — On the Single Name Possessing Multiple Meanings, Being Homonymous in Relation to Them
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الفصل الثالث في الاسم الواحد الذي له معان مختلفة وهو مشترك بالإضافة إليها

كالمؤمن مثلا فإنه قد يراد به المصدق وقد يشتق من الأمن ويكون المراد
إفادة الأمن والأمان فهل يجوز أن يحمل على كلا المعنيين حمل العموم على
مسمياته كما يحمل العليم على العلم بالغيب والشهادة والظاهر والباطن وغير
ذلك من المعلومات الكثيرة وهذا إذا نظر إليه من حيث اللغة فبعيد أن يحمل
الاسم المشترك على جميع المسميات حمل العموم إذ العرب تطلق اسم الرجل وتريد
به كل واحد من الرجال وهذا هو العموم ولا تطلق اسم العين وتريد به عين
الشمس والدينار وعين الميزان والعين المنفجرة من الماء والعين الباصرة من
الحيوان وهذا هو اللفظ المشترك بل تطلق مثل ذلك لإرادة أحد معانيه وتميز
ذلك بالقرينة وقد حكي عن الشافعي رضي الله عنه في الأصول أنه قال الاسم
المشترك يحمل على جميع مسمياته إذا ورد مطلقا ما لم تدل قرينة على التخصيص
وهذا إن صح منه فهو بعيد بل  مطلق لفظ العين مبهم في اللغة لا يتعين به واحد
من مسمياته إلا أن تدل قرينة على التعيين
فأما التعميم فربما خالف وضع الشرع وضع اللسان نعم فيما تصرف الشرع فيه
من الألفاظ لا يبعد أن يكون من وضعه وتصرفه إطلاق اللفظ لإرادة جميع
المعاني فيكون اسم المؤمن بالشرع محمولا على المصدق ومفيدا الأمن بوضع شرعي
لا بوضع لغوي كما أن اسم الصلاة والصيام قد اختص بتصرف الشرع ببعض أمور لا
يقتضي وضع اللغة ذلك فهذا غير بعيد لو كان عليه دليل
ولكن لم يدل دليل على أن الشرع قد غير الوضع فيه والأغلب على ظني أنه لم
يغير وأن من قال من المصنفين إن الاسم الواحد من أسماء الله عز وجل إذا
احتمل معاني ولم يدل العقل على إحالة شيء منها حمل على الجميع بطريق العموم
فقد أبعد فيه
نعم من المعاني ما يتقارب تقاربا يكاد يرجع الاختلاف فيه إلى الإضافات
فيقرب شبهه من العموم فالتعميم فيه أقرب كالسلام فإنه يحتمل أن يكون المراد
سلامته من العيب والنقص ويحتمل أن يكون المراد سلامة الخلق به ومنه فهذا
وأمثاله أشبه بالعموم فإذا ثبت أن الميل الأظهر إلى منع التعميم فطلب
التعيين لبعض المعاني لا يكون إلا بالاجتهاد فيكون الحامل للمجتهد على
تعيين بعض المعاني إما أنه أليق كمفيد الأمان فإنه أليق بالمدح في حق الله
عز وجل من التصديق فإن التصديق أليق بغيره إذ يجب على الكل الإيمان به
والتصديق بكلامه فإن رتبة المصدق فوق رتبة المصدق وإما أن يكون أحد
المعنيين لا يؤدي إلى الترادف بين اسمين كحمل المهيمن على غير الرقيب فإنه
أولى من الرقيب لأن الرقيب قد ورد والترادف بعيد كما ذكرناه وإما أن يكون
أحد المعنيين أظهر في التعارف وأسبق إلى الإفهام لشهرته أو أدل على الكمال
والمدح فهذا وما يجري مجراه ينبغي أن يعول عليه في بيان الأسامي ولا نذكر
لكل اسم إلا معنى واحدا نراه أقرب ونضرب عما عداه صفحا إلا إذا رأيناه
مقاربا  في الدرجة لما ذكرناه فأما تكثير الأقاويل المختلفة فيه مع أنا لا
نرى تعميم الألفاظ المشتركة فلا نرى فيه فائدة

### | الفصل الرابع في بيان أن كمال العبد وسعادته في التخلق بأخلاق الله تعالى والتحلي بمعاني صفاته وأسمائه بقدر ما يتصور في حقه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: أ-م-ن (ʾ-m-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core sense of safety, security, freedom from fear; also ṣidq (veracity) in the form of taṣdīq (affirmation/assent).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, al-muʾmin denotes both the one who affirms (muṣaddiq) and the one who grants security (muʾmin) — a divine attribute entailing bestowal of amān.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage distinguishes the active sense (granting security) from the cognitive sense (believing); homonymy (ishtirāk) is a lexical fact, not a basis for universal predication.
- Root: س-ل-م (s-l-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Freedom from defect (salāmatun min al-ʿayb), and also safety conferred upon others.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Al-Salām as a divine name signifies transcendence above deficiency and the source of creaturely well-being.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): The two senses are near-adjacent, making universal predication more plausible than in distant homonyms.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Contextual Specification (Qarīnah) — In homonymous expressions (mushtarak), the utterance (lafẓ) remains indeterminate (mubham) until a contextual indicator (qarīnah) fixes one referent; universal scope (ʿumūm) is not a default syntactic operation for such nouns.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that a single name may possess multiple meanings and be homonymous (mushtarak) in relation to them — as with "the Faithful" (al-Muʾmin), for instance. It may be intended to mean "the Affirmer" (al-muṣaddiq), or it may be derived from security (al-amn), such that what is intended is the conferral of safety and security (al-amān). Is it then permissible to predicate it upon both meanings in the manner of universal scope (ḥaml al-ʿumūm) over its referents — just as "the Knower" (al-ʿAlīm) is predicated upon knowledge of the unseen and the witnessed, the apparent and the hidden, and the many other things known? Now, when this is considered from the standpoint of language (min ḥaythu al-lughah), it is remote that a homonymous name should be applied to all its referents in the manner of universal scope. For the Arabs utter the word "man" (rajul) intending thereby every single individual among men — and this is genuine universality (ʿumūm). But they do not utter the word "eye" (ʿayn) intending thereby the eye of the sun, the eye of the dinar (i.e., the coin's face), the eye of the balance (i.e., the tongue), the eye gushing forth from water (i.e., a spring), and the seeing eye of the animal — for this is the homonymous expression (al-lafẓ al-mushtarak). Rather, they utter such a word only to intend one of its meanings, and that is distinguished by a contextual indicator (qarīnah).

It has been reported concerning al-Shāfiʿī — may God be pleased with him — in [his work on] legal theory (al-uṣūl) that he said: "The homonymous name is predicated upon all its referents when it occurs absolutely (muṭlaqan), so long as no contextual indicator points to specification (takhṣīṣ)." If this is authentic of him, it is nonetheless remote. Rather, the absolute utterance of "eye" (ʿayn) is indeterminate (mubham) in the language; no single one of its referents is determined by it unless a contextual indicator indicates determination (taʿyīn).

As for universalization (taʿmīm), perhaps the convention of the Sacred Law (waḍʿ al-sharʿ) may diverge from the convention of the tongue (waḍʿ al-lisān). Indeed, in what the Sacred Law has disposed of among expressions, it is not far-fetched that its convention and disposition should consist in uttering the word to intend all its meanings. Thus the name "the Faithful" (al-Muʾmin) would, by the Sacred Law, be predicated upon "the Affirmer" and "the Conferrer of Security" by a legal convention (waḍʿ sharʿī), not by a linguistic convention (waḍʿ lughawī) — just as the names "prayer" (al-ṣalāh) and "fasting" (al-ṣiyām) have been specified, through the disposition of the Sacred Law, to certain matters that the linguistic convention does not require. This, then, is not far-fetched — were there a proof for it.

But no proof has indicated that the Sacred Law has altered the convention in this matter. And the prevailing of my conviction (al-aghallu ʿalā ẓannī) is that it has not altered it. Whoever among the authors has said that a single one of God's names — mighty and majestic is He — when it admits of multiple meanings and the intellect does not indicate the impossibility of any of them, is predicated upon all of them by way of universal scope — such a one has gone far afield (abʿada) therein.

Indeed, among the meanings there are those that approximate one another so closely that the difference between them almost reverts to mere relations (iḍāfāt), such that their resemblance to universality becomes near — and universalization therein is more plausible. Such is "the Peace" (al-Salām): it may be intended that He is free from defect and deficiency (salāmatuhu min al-ʿayb wa-l-naqṣ), and it may be intended that creation is safe through Him and from Him (salāmat al-khalq bihi wa-minhu). This and its like are more akin to universality.

Since it is established that the more manifest inclination is toward prohibiting universalization (manʿ al-taʿmīm), then seeking the determination (taʿyīn) of some meanings can only be through independent reasoning (ijtihād). What impels the one who exercises ijtihād to determine some meanings is either: that it is more fitting (alyaq) — as "the Conferrer of Security" is more fitting as praise (madḥ) with respect to God — mighty and majestic is He — than "the Affirmer," for affirmation (taṣdīq) is more fitting to other than Him, since all are obligated to believe in Him and affirm His speech; for the rank of the one affirmed (al-muṣaddaq) is above the rank of the affirmer (al-muṣaddiq). Or: that one of the two meanings does not lead to synonymy (tarāduf) between two names — as predicating "the Guardian" (al-Muhaymin) upon other than "the Watcher" (al-Raqīb) is more appropriate than [predicating it upon] "the Watcher," because "the Watcher" has already occurred [as a divine name], and synonymy is remote, as we have mentioned. Or: that one of the two meanings is more manifest in common usage (azhar fī al-taʿāruf), more precedent in reaching the understanding (asbaq ilā al-afhām) due to its fame, or more indicative of perfection and praise (adallu ʿalā al-kamāl wa-l-madḥ).

This, and whatever runs its course, is what ought to be relied upon in explaining the names (bayān al-asmāʾ). We shall not mention for each name save a single meaning that we deem most proximate (aqrab), and we shall turn away from what is other than it — except when we see it approximating in degree what we have mentioned. As for multiplying divergent sayings concerning it, given that we do not hold to the universalization of homonymous expressions, we see no benefit in it.

---

### | Section 5 — On the Explanation that the Perfection of the Servant and His Felicity Consist in His Assimilating to the Character Traits of God — Mighty and Majestic Is He — and in His Adorning Himself with the Meanings of His Attributes and Names, to the Extent That Is Conceivable in His Regard

chapters.title_en: The Degrees of Human Share in the Meanings of the Divine Names and the True Nature of Knowledge of God
chapters.arabic_text:
اعلم أن من لم يكن له حظ من معاني أسماء الله عز وجل إلا بأن يسمع لفظه
ويفهم في اللغة معنى تفسيره ووضعه ويعتقد بالقلب وجود معناه في الله تعالى
فهو مبخوس الحظ نازل الدرجة ليس يحسن به أن يتبجح بما ناله فإن سماع اللفظ
لا يستدعي إلا سلامة حاسة السمع التي بها تدرك الأصوات وهذه رتبة تشارك
البهيمة فيها وأما فهم وضعه في اللغة فلا يستدعي إلا معرفة العربية وهذه
رتبة يشارك فيها الأديب اللغوي بل الغبي اللغوي البدوي وأما اعتقاد ثبوت
معناه لله سبحانه وتعالى من غير كشف فلا يستدعي إلا فهم معاني الألفاظ
والتصديق بها وهذه رتبة يشارك فيها العامي بل الصبي فإنه بعد فهم الكلام
إذا ألقي إليه هذه المعاني تلقاها وتلقنها واعتقدها بقلبه وصمم عليها وهذه
درجات أكثر العلماء فضلا عن غيرهم ولا ينكر فضل هؤلاء بالإضافة إلى من لم
يشاركهم في هذه الدرجات الثلاث ولكنه نقص ظاهر بالإضافة إلى ذروة الكمال
فإن حسنات الأبرار سيئات المقربين بل حظوظ المقربين من معاني أسماء الله
تعالى ثلاثة
الحظ الأول معرفة هذه المعاني على سبيل المكاشفة والمشاهدة حتى يتضح لهم
حقائقها بالبرهان الذي لا يجوز فيه الخطأ وينكشف لهم اتصاف الله عز وجل بها
انكشافا يجري في الوضوح والبيان مجرى اليقين الحاصل للإنسان
بصفاته الباطنة التي يدركها بمشاهدة باطنه لا بإحساس ظاهر وكم بين هذا
وبين الاعتقاد المأخوذ من الآباء والمعلمين تقليدا والتصميم عليه وإن كان
مقرونا بأدلة جدلية كلامية
الحظ الثاني من حظوظهم استعظامهم ما ينكشف لهم من صفات الجلال على وجه
ينبعث من الاستعظام يشوقهم إلى الاتصاف بما يمكنهم من تلك الصفات ليقربوا
بها من الحق قربا بالصفة لا بالمكان فيأخذوا من الاتصاف  بها شبها بالملائكة
المقربين عند الله عز وجل ولن يتصور أن يمتلئ القلب باستعظام صفة
واستشرافها إلا ويتبعه شوق إلى تلك الصفة وعشق لذلك الكمال والجلال وحرص
على التحلي بذلك الوصف إن كان ذلك ممكنا للمستعظم بكماله فإن لم يكن بكماله
فينبعث الشوق إلى القدر الممكن منه لا محالة
ولا يخلو عن هذا الشوق أحد إلا لأحد أمرين إما لضعف المعرفة واليقين بكون
الوصف المعلوم من أوصاف الجلال والكمال وإما لكون القلب ممتلئا بشوق آخر
مستغرقا به فالتلميذ إذا شاهد كمال أستاذه في العلم انبعث شوقه إلى التشبه
والاقتداء به إلا إذا كان مملوءا بالجوع مثلا فإن استغراق باطنه بشوق القوت
ربما يمنع انبعاث شوق العلم ولهذا ينبغي أن يكون الناظر في صفات الله تعالى
خاليا بقلبه عن إرادة ما سوى الله عز وجل فإن المعرفة بذر الشوق ولكن مهما
صادف قلبا خاليا عن حسيكة الشهوات فإن لم يكن خاليا لم يكن البذر منجحا
الحظ الثالث السعي في اكتساب الممكن من تلك الصفات والتخلق بها والتحلي
بمحاسنها وبه يصير العبد ربانيا أي قريبا من الرب تعالى وبه يصير رفيقا
للملأ الأعلى من الملائكة فإنهم على بساط القرب فمن ضرب إلى شبه من صفاتهم
نال شيئا من قربهم بقدر ما نال من أوصافهم المقربة لهم إلى الحق تعالى
فإن قلت طلب القرب من الله عز وجل بالصفة أمر غامض تكاد تشمئز القلوب عن
قبوله والتصديق به فزده شرحا تكسر به سورة إنكار المنكرين فإن هذا كالمنكر
عند الأكثرين إن لم تكشف حقيقته فأقول لا يخفى عليك ولا على من ترعرع قليلا
من درجة عوام العلماء أن الموجودات منقسمة إلى كاملة وناقصة والكامل أشرف
من الناقص ومهما تفاوتت درجات الكمال واقتصر منتهى الكمال على واحد حتى لم
يكن الكمال المطلق إلا له ولم يكن للموجودات الأخر كمال مطلق بل كانت لها
كمالات متفاوتة بالإضافة فأكملها أقرب لا محالة إلى الذي له الكمال المطلق
أعني قربا بالرتبة والدرجة لا بالكمال
ثم الموجودات منقسمة  إلى حية وميتة وتعلم أن الحي أشرف وأكمل من الميت
وأن درجات الأحياء ثلاثة درجة الملائكة ودرجة الإنس ودرجة البهائم ودرجة
البهائم أسفل في نفس الحياة التي بها شرفها لأن الحي هو الدراك الفعال وفي
إدراك البهيمة نقص وفي فعلها نقص أما إدراكها فنقصانه أنه مقصور على الحواس
وإدراك الحس قاصر لأنه لا يدرك الأشياء إلا بمماسة أو بقرب منها فالحس
معزول عن الإدراك إن لم يكن مماسة ولا قرب فإن الذوق واللمس يحتاجان إلى
المماسة والسمع والبصر والشم يحتاج إلى القرب وكل موجود لا يتصور فيه
المماسة والقرب فالحس معزول عن إدراكه في الحال وأما فعلها فهو أنه مقصور
على مقتضى الشهوة والغضب لا باعث لها سواهما وليس لها عقل يدعو إلى أفعال
مخالفة لمقتضى الشهوة والغضب
وأما الملك فدرجته أعلى الدرجات لأنه عبارة عن موجود لا يؤثر القرب
والبعد في إدراكه بل لا يقتصر إدراكه على ما يتصور فيه القرب والبعد إذ
القرب والبعد يتصور على الأجسام والأجسام أخس أقسام الموجودات ثم هو مقدس
عن الشهوة والغضب فليست أفعاله بمقتضى الشهوة والغضب بل داعيه
إلى الأفعال أمر أجل من الشهوة والغضب وهو طلب التقرب إلى الله عز وجل
وأما الإنسان فإن درجته متوسطة بين الدرجتين وكأنه مركب من بهيمية وملكية
والأغلب عليه في بداية أمره البهيمية إذ ليس له أولا من الإدراك إلا الحواس
التي يحتاج في الإدراك بها إلى طلب القرب من المحسوس بالسعي والحركة إلى أن
يشرق عليه بالآخرة نور العقل المتصرف في ملكوت السموات والأرض من غير حاجة
إلى حركة بالبدن وطلب قرب أو مماسة مع المدرك به بل مدركه الأمور المقدسة
عن قبول القرب والبعد بالمكان وكذلك المستولي عليه أولا شهوته وغضبه وبحسب
مقتضاهما انبعاثه إلى أن يظهر فيه الرغبة في طلب الكمال والنظر للعاقبة
وعصيان مقتضى الشهوة والغضب فإن غلب الشهوة والغضب حتى ملكهما وضعفا عن
تحريكه وتسكينه أخذ بذلك شبها من الملائكة وكذلك إن فطم نفسه عن الجمود على
الخيالات والمحسوسات وأنس  بإدراك أمور تجل عن أن ينالها حس أو خيال أخذ
شبها أخر من الملائكة فإن خاصية الحياة الإدراك والعقل وإليهما يتطرق
النقصان والتوسط والكمال ومهما اقتدى بالملائكة في هاتين الخاصيتين كان
أبعد عن البهيمية وأقرب من الملك والملك قريب من الله عز وجل والقريب من
القريب قريب
فإن قلت فظاهر هذا الكلام يشير إلى إثبات مشابهة بين العبد وبين الله
تعالى لأنه إذا تخلق بأخلاقه كان شبيها له ومعلوم شرعا وعقلا أن الله
سبحانه وتعالى ليس كمثله شيء وأنه لا يشبه شيئا ولا يشبهه شيء فأقول مهما
عرفت معنى المماثلة المنفية عن الله عز وجل عرفت أنه لا مثل له ولا ينبغي
أن يظن أن المشاركة في كل وصف توجب المماثلة
افترى أن الضدين يتماثلان وبينهما غاية البعد الذي لا يتصور أن يكون بعد
فوقه وهما متشاركان في أوصاف كثيرة إذ السواد يشارك البياض في كونه عرضا
وفي كونه لونا وفي كونه مدركا بالبصر وأمور أخر سواها أفترى أن من قال إن
الله عز وجل موجود لا في محل وإنه سميع بصير عالم مريد متكلم حي قادر فاعل
والإنسان أيضا كذلك فقد شبه وأثبت المثل هيهات ليس الأمر كذلك ولو كان كذلك
لكان الخلق كلهم مشبهة إذ لا أقل من إثبات المشاركة في الوجود وهو موهم
للمشابهة بل المماثلة عبارة عن المشاركة في النوع والماهية والفرس وإن كان
بالغا في الكياسة لا يكون مثلا للإنسان لأنه مخالف له بالنوع وإنما يشابهه
بالكياسة التي هي عارضة خارجة عن الماهية المقومة لذات الإنسانية
والخاصية الإلهية أنه الموجود الواجب الوجود بذاته الذي عنه يوجد كل ما
في الإمكان وجوده على أحسن وجوه النظام والكمال وهذه الخاصية لا يتصور فيها
مشاركة البتة والمماثلة بها لا تحصل فكون العبد رحيما صبورا شكورا لا يوجب
المماثلة ككونه سمعيا بصيرا عالما قادرا حيا فاعلا بل أقول الخاصية الإلهية
ليست إلا لله تعالى ولا يعرفها إلا الله ولا يتصور أن يعرفها إلا هو أو من
هو مثله وإذا  لم يكن له مثل فلا يعرفها غيره فإذا الحق ما قاله الجنيد رحمه
الله حيث قال لا يعرف الله إلا الله ولذلك لم يعط أجل خلقه إلا اسما حجبه
به فقال {سبح اسم ربك الأعلى} 87 سورة الأعلى الآية 1 فوالله ما عرف الله
غير الله في الدنيا والآخرة وقيل لذي النون وقد أشرف على الموت ماذا تشتهي
فقال أن أعرفه قبل أن أموت ولو بلحظة وهذا الآن يشوش قلوب أكثر الضعفاء
ويوهم عندهم القول بالنفي والتعطيل وذلك لعجزهم عن فهم هذا الكلام
وأنا أقول لو قال القائل لا أعرف الله كان صادقا ولو قال أعرف الله كان
صادقا ومعلوم أن النفي والإثبات لا يصدقان معا بل يتقاسمان
الصدق والكذب فإن صدق النفي كذب الإثبات وبالعكس ولكن إذا اختلف وجه
الكلام تصور الصدق في القسمين وهو كما لو قال القائل لغيره هل تعرف الصديق
أبا بكر رضي الله عنه فقال والصديق ممن يجهل ولا يعرف أو يتصور في العالم
من لا يعرفه مع ظهوره واشتهاره وانتشار اسمه فهل على المنابر إلا حديثه وهل
في المساجد إلا ذكره وهل على الألسنة إلا ثناؤه ووصفه لكان هذا القائل
صادقا ولو قيل لآخر هل تعرفه فقال ومن أنا حتى أعرف الصديق هيهات لا يعرف
الصديق سوى الصديق أو من هو مثله أو فوقه ومن أين لي أن أدعي معرفته أو
أطمع فيها وإنما مثلي يسمع اسمه وصفته فأما أن يدعي معرفته فذلك محال فهذا
أيضا صادق وله وجه وهو أقرب إلى التعظيم والاحترام
وهكذا ينبغي أن يفهم قول من قال أعرف الله وقول من قال لا أعرف الله
بل لو عرضت خطا منظوما على عاقل وقلت هل تعرف كاتبه فقال لا صدق ولو قال
نعم كاتبه هو الإنسان الحي القادر السميع البصير السليم اليد العالم بصناعة
الكتابة فإذا عرفت كل هذا منه فكيف لا أعرفه فهذا أيضا صدق ولكن الأحق
والأصدق قوله لا أعرفه فإنه بالحقيقة ما عرفه وإنما عرف احتياج الخط
المنظوم  إلى كاتب حي عالم قادر سميع بصير سليم اليد عالم بصناعة الكتابة
ولم يعرف الكاتب نفسه فكذلك الخلق كلهم لم يعرفوا إلا احتياج هذا العالم
المنظوم المحكم إلى صانع مدبر حي عالم قادر
وهذه المعرفة لها طرفان أحدهما يتعلق بالعالم ومعلومه احتياجه إلى مدبر
والآخر يتعلق بالله عز وجل ومعلومه أسامي مشتقة من صفات غير داخلة في حقيقة
الذات وماهيتها فإنا قد بينا أنه إذا أشار المشير إلى شيء
وقال ما هو لم يكن ذكر الأسماء المشتقة جوابا أصلا فلو أشار إلى شخص
حيوان فقال ما هو فقيل طويل أو أبيض أو قصير أو أشار إلى ماء فقال ما هو
فقيل بأنه بارد أو أشار إلى نار وقال ما هو فقيل حار فكل ذلك ليس بجواب عن
الماهية البتة والمعرفة بالشيء هي معرفة حقيقته وماهيته لا معرفة الأسامي
المشتقة فإن قولنا حار معناه شيء مبهم له وصف الحرارة وكذلك قولنا قادر
وعالم معناه شيء مبهم له وصف العلم والقدرة
فإن قلت فقولنا إنه الواجب الوجود الذي عنه وحده يوجد كل ما في الإمكان
وجوده عبارة عن حقيقته وحده وقد عرفنا هذا فأقول هيهات فقولنا واجب الوجود
عبارة عن استغنائه عن العلة والفاعل وهذا يرجع إلى سلب السبب عنه وقولنا
يوجد عنه كل موجود يرجع إلى إضافة الأفعال إليه وإذا قيل لنا ما هذا الشيء
وقلنا هو الفاعل لم يكن جوابا وإذا قلنا هو الذي له علة لم يكن جوابا فكيف
قولنا هو الذي لا علة له لأن كل ذلك نبأ عن غير ذاته وعن إضافة له إلى ذاته
إما بنفي أو إثبات وكل ذلك أسماء وصفات وإضافات
فإن قلت فما السبيل إلى معرفته فأقول لو قال لنا صبي أو عنين ما السبيل
إلى معرفة لذة الوقاع وإدراك حقيقته قلنا هاهنا سبيلان أحدهما أن نصفه لك
حتى تعرفه والآخر أن تصبر حتى تظهر فيك غريزة الشهوة ثم تباشر الوقاع حتى
تظهر فيك لذة الوقاع فتعرفه وهذا السبيل الثاني هو السبيل المحقق  المفضي
إلى حقيقة المعرفة
فأما الأول فلا يفضي إلا إلى توهم وتشبيه للشيء بما لا يشبهه إذ غايتنا
أن نمثل لذة الوقاع عنده بشيء من اللذات التي يدركها العنين كلذة الطعام
والشراب الحلو مثلا فنقول له أما تعرف أن السكر لذيذ فإنك تجد عند تناوله
حالة طيبة وتحس في نفسك راحة قال نعم قلنا فالجماع أيضا كذلك أفترى أن هذا
يفهمه حقيقة لذة الجماع كما هي حتى ينزل في معرفته منزلة من ذاق تلك اللذة
وأدركها هيهات إنما غاية هذا الوصف إيهام وتشبيه خطأ وتفهيم ومشاركة في
الاسم
أما الإيهام فهو أنه يتوهم أن ذلك أمر طيب على الجملة وأما التشبيه فهو
أنه يشبهه بحلاوة السكر وهو خطأ إذ لا مناسبة بين حلاوة السكر ولذة الوقاع
وأما المشاركة في الاسم فهو أنه يعلم أنه مستحق أن يسمى لذة ومهما ظهرت
الشهوة وذاق علم قطعا أنه لا يشبهه حلاوة السكر وأن ما كان توهمه لم يكن
على الوجه الذي توهمه نعم يعلم أن الذي كان قد سمع من اسمه وصفته وأنه لذيذ
وطيب كان صادقا بل كان أصدق عليه منه على حلاوة السكر
فكذلك لمعرفة الله سبحانه وتعالى سبيلان أحدهما قاصر والآخر مسدود
أما القاصر فهو ذكر الأسماء والصفات وطريقة التشبيه بما عرفناه من أنفسنا
فإنا لما عرفنا أنفسنا قادرين عالمين أحياء متكلمين ثم سمعنا ذلك في أوصاف
الله عز وجل أو عرفناه بالدليل فهمناه فهما قاصرا كفهم العنين لذة الوقاع
بما يوصف له من لذة السكر بل حياتنا وقدرتنا وعلمنا أبعد من حياة الله عز
وجل وقدرته وعلمه من حلاوة السكر من لذة الوقاع بل لا مناسبة بين البعيدين
وفائدة تعريف الله عز وجل بهذه الأوصاف أيضا إيهام وتشبيه ومشاركة في الاسم
لكن يقطع التشبيه بأن يقال ليس كمثله شيء فهو حي لا كالأحياء وقادر لا
كالقادرين كما تقول الوقاع لذيذ كالسكر ولكن تلك اللذة لا تشبه هذه البتة
ولكن تشاركها في الاسم
وكأنا إذا عرفنا أن الله تعالى حي  قادر عالم فلم نعرف إلا أنفسنا ولم
نعرفه إلا بأنفسنا إذ الأصم لا يتصور أن يفهم معنى قولنا إن الله سميع ولا
الأكمه يفهم معنى قولنا إنه بصير ولذلك إذا قال القائل كيف يكون الله عز
وجل عالما بالأشياء فنقول كما تعلم أنت الأشياء فإذا قال فكيف يكون قادرا
فنقول كما تقدر أنت فلا يمكنه أن يفهم شيئا إلا إذا كان فيه ما يناسبه
فيعلم أولا ما هو متصف به ثم يعلم غيره بالمقايسة إليه فإن كان لله عز وجل
وصف وخاصية ليس فينا ما يناسبه ويشاركه في الاسم ولو مشاركة حلاوة السكر
لذة الوقاع لم يتصور فهمه البتة فما عرف أحد إلا نفسه ثم قايس بين صفات
الله تعالى وصفات نفسه وتتعالى صفاته عن أن تشبه صفاتنا فتكون هذه معرفة
قاصرة يغلب عليها الإيهام والتشبيه فينبغي أن تقترن بها المعرفة بنفي
المشابهة وينفي أصل المناسبة مع المشاركة في الاسم
وأما السبيل الثاني المسدود فهو أن ينتظر العبد أن تحصل له الصفات
الربوبية كلها حتى يصير ربا كما ينتظر الصبي أن يبلغ فيدرك تلك اللذة وهذا
السبيل مسدود ممتنع إذ يستحيل أن تحصل تلك الحقيقة لغير الله تعالى وهذا هو
سبيل المعرفة المحققة لا غير وهو مسدود قطعا إلا على الله تعالى
فإذا يستحيل أن يعرف الله تعالى بالحقيقة غير الله بل أقول يستحيل أن
يعرف النبي غير النبي وأما من لا نبوة له فلا يعرف من النبوة إلا اسمها
وأنها خاصية موجودة لإنسان بها يفارق من ليس نبيا ولكن لا يعرف ماهية تلك
الخاصية إلا بالتشبيه بصفات نفسه
بل أزيد وأقول لا يعرف أحد حقيقة الموت وحقيقة الجنة والنار إلا بعد
الموت ودخول الجنة أو النار لأن الجنة عبارة عن أسباب ملذة ولو فرضنا شخصا
لم يدرك قط لذة لم يمكننا أصلا أن نفهمه الجنة تفهيما يرغبه في طلبها
والنار عبارة عن أسباب مؤلمة ولو فرضنا شخصا لم يقاس قط ألما لم يمكننا
قط أن نفهمه النار فإذا قاساه  فهمناه إياه بالتشبيه بأشد ما قاساه وهو ألم
النار
وكذلك إذا أدرك شيئا من اللذات فغايتنا أن نفهمه الجنة بالتشبيه بأعظم ما
ناله من اللذات وهي المطعم والمنكح والمنظر فإن كان في الجنة لذة مخالفة
لهذه اللذات فلا سبيل إلى تفهيمه أصلا إلا بالتشبيه بهذه اللذات كما ذكرناه
في تشبيه لذة الوقاع بحلاوة السكر ولذات الجنة أبعد من كل لذة أدركناها في
الدنيا من لذة الوقاع عن لذة السكر بل العبارة الصحيحة عنها أنها ما لا عين
رأت ولا أذن سمعت ولا خطر على قلب بشر فإن مثلناها بالأطعمة قلنا مع ذلك لا
كهذه الأطعمة وإن مثلناها بالوقاع قلنا لا كالوقاع المعهود في الدنيا فكيف

chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح-ظ (ḥ-ẓ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Portion, share, allotment of good fortune; that which falls to one's lot.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The portion of knowledge or beatitude apportioned to a servant; used here for the graded shares of the divine names' meanings.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of a fixed share; metaphorically extended to the intellectual and spiritual allotment of comprehension.
- Root: ك-ش-ف (k-sh-f)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Removal of a covering; unveiling, disclosure.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Direct, immediate apprehension of divine realities granted to the saints (mukāshafah), contrasted with taqlīd (imitation).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: lifting a veil; metaphorical: the heart's direct vision of metaphysical truths without intermediary.
- Root: م-ث-ل (m-th-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Likeness, similitude, equivalent.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The theological crux of tashbīh (anthropomorphism) vs. tanzīh (transcendence); God's incomparability (laysa ka-mithlihi shay').
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal: exact resemblance in essence; metaphorical: mere nominal or partial participation in attributes, which does not entail likeness.
- Sībawayh Rule: Taqābūl al-Ḍiddayn (Contrast of Opposites) — The rule governing the reconciliation of seemingly contradictory propositions (e.g., "I know God" and "I do not know God") by distinguishing the aspects (wajh) of each predication, as in {«وما رميت إذ رميت ولكن الله رمى»}.
chapters.translation:
I say: Know that whoever has no share of the meanings of God's names—mighty and majestic is He—except that he hears their utterance, understands in language the sense of their interpretation and their conventional usage, and believes in his heart that their meaning subsists in God—exalted is He—such a one is meager in share, low in rank, and it does not befit him to boast of what he has attained. For hearing the utterance requires only the soundness of the sense of hearing by which sounds are perceived—and this is a rank in which the beast shares with him. As for understanding its conventional usage in language, that requires only knowledge of Arabic—and this is a rank in which the literary scholar shares, nay even the dull-witted Bedouin linguist. As for believing that its meaning is firmly established for God—glorified and exalted is He—without unveiling, that requires only understanding the meanings of the words and assenting to them—and this is a rank in which the common man shares, nay even the child, for after understanding speech, if these meanings are cast to him, he receives them, learns them, believes them in his heart, and is firmly resolved upon them. These are the degrees of most scholars, let alone others. The merit of these people relative to those who do not share with them in these three degrees is not denied—but it is an evident deficiency relative to the summit of perfection, for the good deeds of the righteous are the sins of those brought near (ḥasanāt al-abrār sayyi'āt al-muqarrabīn).

Rather, the shares of those brought near from the meanings of God's names—exalted is He—are three:

**The First Share**: Knowledge of these meanings by way of unveiling (mukāshafah) and direct witnessing (mushāhadah), so that their realities become clear to them through a demonstration (burhān) in which error is impossible, and the attribution of these meanings to God—mighty and majestic is He—is disclosed to them with a disclosure that runs, in clarity and evidentness, to the level of the certainty a man has of his own inner attributes, which he perceives by witnessing his inner self, not by outward sensation. How vast is the distance between this and the belief taken from fathers and teachers by imitation (taqlīd) and firm resolve upon it, even if it be accompanied by dialectical theological proofs!

**The Second Share** of their shares: Their magnification (istiʿẓām) of what is disclosed to them of the attributes of majesty (ṣifāt al-jalāl) in a manner that, from this magnification, there is kindled in them a longing (shawq) to be characterized by whatever of those attributes is possible for them, so that thereby they draw near to the Truth—a nearness by attribute, not by place. Thus they take from being characterized by them a resemblance to the angels brought near to God—mighty and majestic is He. It is inconceivable that the heart be filled with magnification of an attribute and aspiration toward it without there following from it a longing for that attribute, a passion for that perfection and majesty, and an eagerness to be adorned with that description—if that is possible for the one who magnifies it in its completeness. But if not in its completeness, then the longing is kindled for the possible measure of it, inevitably.

None is devoid of this longing except for one of two reasons: either the weakness of knowledge and certainty that the known description is among the attributes of majesty and perfection, or the heart's being filled with another longing that overwhelms it. For the student, when he witnesses the perfection of his teacher in knowledge, his longing to resemble him and follow his example is kindled—unless he is filled, for instance, with hunger, for the absorption of his inner self in the longing for sustenance may prevent the kindling of the longing for knowledge. For this reason, the one who contemplates the attributes of God—exalted is He—should have his heart empty of willing anything other than God—mighty and majestic is He—for knowledge is the seed of longing, but whenever it encounters a heart empty of the thorns of appetites, it thrives; if it is not empty, the seed does not prosper.

**The Third Share**: Striving to acquire what is possible of those attributes, being characterized by them (takhalluq), and adorning oneself with their excellences. By this, the servant becomes lordly (rabbānī), that is, near to the Lord—exalted is He—and by this he becomes a companion of the most exalted assembly of angels, for they are upon the carpet of nearness. Whoever strikes toward resemblance to some of their attributes attains something of their nearness, to the measure of what he attains of their attributes that bring them near to the Truth—exalted is He.

If you say: "The seeking of nearness to God—mighty and majestic is He—by attribute is an obscure matter from which hearts almost recoil in acceptance and assent; so increase its explanation in a way that breaks the force of the deniers' rejection, for this is like something rejected by most people unless its reality is unveiled"—then I say: It is not hidden from you, nor from anyone who has grown up a little above the rank of the common run of scholars, that existing things are divided into the perfect and the deficient, and the perfect is nobler than the deficient. Whenever the degrees of perfection are differentiated and the utmost limit of perfection is confined to one alone, so that absolute perfection belongs to none but Him, and other existents have no absolute perfection but rather have perfections that are relative and differentiated—then the most perfect of them is inevitably the nearest to the One to whom belongs absolute perfection, I mean nearness in rank and degree, not in perfection.

Then existing things are divided into the living and the dead, and you know that the living is nobler and more perfect than the dead, and that the degrees of the living are three: the degree of the angels, the degree of humans, and the degree of beasts. The degree of beasts is the lowest in the very life by which they are ennobled, because the living is the perceiving, the acting. In the beast's perception there is deficiency, and in its action there is deficiency. As for its perception, its deficiency is that it is confined to the senses, and sense-perception is deficient because it perceives things only by contact or by proximity to them. Thus sense is cut off from perception if there is neither contact nor proximity—for taste and touch require contact, while hearing, sight, and smell require proximity—and every existent in which contact and proximity are inconceivable, sense is cut off from perceiving it in that state. As for its action, it is confined to what appetite and anger require; it has no motive other than them, and it has no intellect calling it to acts contrary to what appetite and anger require.

As for the angel, its degree is the highest of degrees, because it is an existent for which proximity and distance have no effect on its perception; rather, its perception is not confined to what admits of proximity and distance, since proximity and distance are conceivable only for bodies, and bodies are the basest of the divisions of existents. Moreover, it is sanctified from appetite and anger, so its acts are not in accordance with appetite and anger; rather, its motive to acts is something more august than appetite and anger—namely, the seeking of nearness to God—mighty and majestic is He.

As for the human, his degree is intermediate between the two degrees. It is as though he is composed of bestiality and angelicity. What predominates over him at the beginning of his affair is bestiality, since at first he has of perception only the senses, by which he needs, in perceiving, to seek proximity to the sensed object by exertion and movement—until finally there dawns upon him the light of the intellect that disposes in the kingdom of the heavens and the earth without need of bodily movement or seeking proximity or contact with the perceived object. Rather, what he perceives are matters sanctified from admitting proximity and distance in place. Likewise, what predominates over him at first is his appetite and his anger, and his impulses are in accordance with their requirements—until there appears in him the desire to seek perfection, regard for the ultimate consequence, and disobedience to what appetite and anger require. If he overcomes appetite and anger until he masters them and they become too weak to move him or still him, he thereby takes on a resemblance to the angels. Likewise, if he weans his soul from being frozen upon imaginings and sensibles and becomes familiar with perceiving matters too sublime for sense or imagination to attain, he takes on another resemblance to the angels. For the specific property of life is perception and intellect, and it is to these two that deficiency, intermediacy, and perfection attach. Whenever he emulates the angels in these two properties, he becomes farther from bestiality and nearer to the angel—and the angel is near to God—mighty and majestic is He—and the near to the near is near.

If you say: "The outward purport of this discourse indicates the affirmation of a resemblance (mushābahah) between the servant and God—exalted is He—for if he is characterized by His character traits, he becomes similar to Him; and it is known by law and by reason that God—glorified and exalted is He—has nothing like unto Him, that He resembles nothing and nothing resembles Him"—then I say: Whenever you understand the meaning of the likeness (mumāthalah) that is negated of God—mighty and majestic is He—you will know that He has no like, and it should not be supposed that participation in every attribute entails likeness.

Do you think that two opposites are alike, between which there is the utmost distance beyond which no greater distance is conceivable—yet they share in many attributes? For blackness shares with whiteness in being an accident, in being a color, in being perceived by sight, and in other matters besides. Do you think that one who says "God—mighty and majestic is He—is an existent not in a locus, and He is hearing, seeing, knowing, willing, speaking, living, powerful, acting—and the human is also so"—has thereby likened and affirmed a like? Far from it! It is not so. Were it so, all creatures would be anthropomorphists (mushabbihah), since there is no less than the affirmation of participation in existence, which suggests resemblance. Rather, likeness (mumāthalah) is participation in species and quiddity (al-nawʿ wa al-māhiyyah). The horse, even if it reaches the utmost in cleverness, is not a like of the human, because it differs from him in species; it merely resembles him in cleverness, which is an accident external to the quiddity that constitutes the essence of humanity.

The divine specific property (al-khāṣṣiyyah al-ilāhiyyah) is that He is the existent necessary of existence in Himself (al-mawjūd al-wājib al-wujūd bi-dhātihi), from whom comes into existence everything whose existence is possible, upon the most excellent manner of order and perfection. This specific property admits of no participation whatsoever, and likeness is not obtained through it. So the servant's being merciful, patient, and thankful does not entail likeness, just as his being hearing, seeing, knowing, powerful, living, and acting does not. Rather, I say: The divine specific property belongs to none but God—exalted is He—and none knows it but God. It is inconceivable that any know it save Him or one like Him; and since He has no like, none other than He knows it. Thus the truth is what al-Junayd—may God have mercy on him—said: "None knows God but God." For this reason, He gave to the most august of His creatures only a name by which He veiled Him, saying: {«سبح اسم ربك الأعلى»} (Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High) — Surah al-Aʿlā, verse 1. By God, none has known God but God, in this world and the next. It was said to Dhū al-Nūn—when he was on the verge of death—"What do you desire?" He said: "That I might know Him before I die, even for a moment." And this now disturbs the hearts of most of the weak and suggests to them the affirmation of negation and suspension (taʿṭīl)—and that is because of their incapacity to understand this discourse.

And I say: If one says "I do not know God," he is truthful; and if one says "I know God," he is truthful. It is known that negation and affirmation are not both true together; rather, they divide truth and falsehood between them—if the negation is true, the affirmation is false, and vice versa. But when the aspect (wajh) of the discourse differs, truth is conceivable in both divisions. This is like when one says to another: "Do you know al-Ṣiddīq, Abū Bakr—may God be pleased with him?" and he replies: "And is al-Ṣiddīq one who is unknown and unrecognized? Or is it conceivable in the world that anyone does not know him, given his prominence, his fame, and the spread of his name? Is there anything on the pulpits but his account? Is there anything in the mosques but his mention? Is there anything on tongues but his praise and description?"—this speaker would be truthful. And if it were said to another: "Do you know him?" and he replied: "And who am I that I should know al-Ṣiddīq? Far from it! None knows al-Ṣiddīq but al-Ṣiddīq, or one like him, or one above him. Whence have I that I should claim knowledge of him or aspire to it? My like merely hears his name and his description; as for claiming knowledge of him, that is impossible"—this one too is truthful, and has an aspect, and it is closer to veneration and reverence.

Thus should be understood the saying of him who says "I know God" and the saying of him who says "I do not know God." Nay, if a well-composed script were displayed to a rational man and you said: "Do you know its writer?" and he said "No," he would be truthful; and if he said "Yes, its writer is the human, the living, the powerful, the hearing, the seeing, sound of hand, knowing the craft of writing—so when I have known all this of him, how do I not know him?"—this too is truthful. But the more fitting and truer is his saying "I do not know him," for in reality he did not know him; he only knew that the well-composed script requires a writer who is living, knowing, powerful, hearing, seeing, sound of hand, knowing the craft of writing—and he did not know the writer himself. Likewise, all creatures have known only that this well-composed, well-ordered world requires a Maker, a Disposer, living, knowing, powerful.

This knowledge has two extremities: one pertains to the world, and its known content is its need for a Disposer; the other pertains to God—mighty and majestic is He—and its known content is names derived from attributes that do not enter into the reality of the Essence and its quiddity. For we have explained that when one points to something and says "What is it?", the mention of derived names is not an answer at all. If one pointed to a living person and said "What is it?" and it was said "Tall, or white, or short"; or pointed to water and said "What is it?" and it was said "It is cold"; or pointed to fire and said "What is it?" and it was said "It is hot"—all of that is not an answer about the quiddity at all. Knowledge of a thing is knowledge of its reality and quiddity, not knowledge of derived names. For our saying "hot" means an indeterminate thing having the attribute of heat; likewise our saying "powerful" and "knowing" means an indeterminate thing having the attributes of knowledge and power.

If you say: "Then our saying that He is the necessary of existence, from whom alone comes into existence everything whose existence is possible—is an expression of His reality alone, and we have known this"—then I say: Far from it! Our saying "necessary of existence" is an expression of His self-sufficiency from cause and agent, and this reverts to the negation of cause from Him. Our saying "from Him comes into existence every existent" reverts to the attribution of acts to Him. When it is said to us "What is this thing?" and we say "He is the agent," that is not an answer; and when we say "He is the one who has a cause," that is not an answer—so how about our saying "He is the one who has no cause"? For all of that is news about other than His Essence, and about an attribution of His Essence, either by negation or affirmation—and all of that is names, attributes, and relations (idāfāt).

If you say: "Then what is the way to knowledge of Him?"—I say: If a child or an impotent man (ʿinnīn) said to us: "What is the way to knowledge of the pleasure of intercourse and the apprehension of its reality?" we would say: Here there are two ways: one is that we describe it to you until you know it; the other is that you be patient until the instinct of appetite appears in you, then you engage in intercourse until the pleasure of intercourse appears in you, and so you know it. This second way is the verified way that leads to the reality of knowledge.

As for the first, it leads only to imagination (tawahhum) and a likening of the thing to what does not resemble it. For our utmost is to represent the pleasure of intercourse to him by something of the pleasures the impotent man perceives, like the pleasure of sweet food and drink, for example. We say to him: "Do you not know that sugar is pleasurable? For you find upon consuming it a pleasant state and feel in yourself a comfort." He says "Yes." We say: "Then intercourse is likewise." Do you think this makes him understand the reality of the pleasure of intercourse as it is, so that he descends in knowledge of it to the station of one who has tasted that pleasure and apprehended it? Far from it! The utmost of this description is illusion (īhām), erroneous likening, making understood, and participation in the name.

As for the illusion, it is that he imagines it to be a pleasant matter in general. As for the likening, it is that he likens it to the sweetness of sugar—and that is an error, for there is no proportion (munāsabah) between the sweetness of sugar and the pleasure of intercourse. As for the participation in the name, it is that he knows it deserves to be called "pleasure." And when the appetite appears and he tastes it, he knows with certainty that the sweetness of sugar does not resemble it, and that what he had imagined was not in the manner he had imagined. Yes, he knows that what he had heard of its name and description—that it is pleasurable and pleasant—was true; rather, it was truer of it than of the sweetness of sugar.

Likewise, for knowledge of God—glorified and exalted is He—there are two ways: one deficient (qāṣir) and one blocked (masdūd).

As for the deficient, it is the mention of names and attributes and the method of likening to what we have known of ourselves. For when we have known ourselves to be powerful, knowing, living, speaking, then heard that of God's attributes—mighty and majestic is He—or known it by proof, we understand it with a deficient understanding, like the impotent man's understanding of the pleasure of intercourse through what is described to him of the pleasure of sugar. Nay, our life, power, and knowledge are farther from God's life, power, and knowledge than the sweetness of sugar is from the pleasure of intercourse; indeed, there is no proportion between the two distant things. The benefit of making God known—exalted is He—through these attributes is also illusion, likening, and participation in the name. But the likening is cut off by saying: "There is nothing like unto Him"—He is living, not like the living; powerful, not like the powerful—just as you say "Intercourse is pleasurable like sugar," but that pleasure does not resemble this one at all; it merely shares with it in the name.

It is as though, when we know that God—exalted is He—is living, powerful, knowing, we have known only ourselves, and have not known Him except through ourselves. For the deaf cannot conceivably understand the meaning of our saying that God is hearing, nor can the blind understand the meaning of our saying that He is seeing. For this reason, when one says "How is God—mighty and majestic is He—knowing of things?" we say: "Just as you know things." And if he says "How is He powerful?" we say: "Just as you are powerful." He cannot understand anything unless there is in him something proportionate to it. So he first knows what he himself is characterized by, then knows other things by analogy to it. If God—mighty and majestic is He—has an attribute and specific property for which there is nothing in us proportionate to it or sharing with it in the name—even the sharing of the sweetness of sugar with the pleasure of intercourse—then its understanding is not conceivable at all. So none has known anything but himself, then drawn an analogy between God's attributes—exalted is He—and his own attributes; and His attributes are too exalted to resemble our attributes. Thus this is a deficient knowledge, dominated by illusion and likening, and it should be coupled with the knowledge of negating resemblance and negating the principle of proportion, along with participation in the name.

As for the second way, the blocked one, it is that the servant wait for all the lordly attributes to be obtained by him until he becomes a lord—just as the child waits to reach maturity and apprehend that pleasure. This way is blocked and impossible, for it is impossible that that reality be obtained by other than God—exalted is He. This is the way of verified knowledge, and none other; and it is blocked absolutely—except for God—exalted is He.

Thus it is impossible that God—exalted is He—be known in reality by other than God. Rather, I say: It is impossible that the Prophet be known by other than a prophet. As for one who has no prophethood, he knows of prophethood only its name—that it is a specific property subsisting in a human by which he is distinguished from one who is not a prophet—but he does not know the quiddity of that specific property except by likening to his own attributes.

Nay, I add and say: No one knows the reality of death, or the reality of Paradise and Hell, except after death and entering Paradise or Hell. For Paradise is an expression of causes of pleasure; and if we supposed a person who had never perceived any pleasure, we could not possibly make him understand Paradise in a way that would make him desire to seek it. And Hell is an expression of causes of pain; and if we supposed a person who had never experienced any pain, we could never make him understand Hell. When he has experienced pain, we make him understand it by likening it to the most severe pain he has experienced—and that is the pain of fire.

Likewise, if he has apprehended something of pleasures, our utmost is to make him understand Paradise by likening it to the greatest of what he has attained of pleasures—namely, food, marriage, and sight. If there is in Paradise a pleasure different from these pleasures, there is no way to make him understand it at all except by likening it to these pleasures, as we mentioned in likening the pleasure of intercourse to the sweetness of sugar. And the pleasures of Paradise are farther from every pleasure we have apprehended in this world than the pleasure of intercourse is from the pleasure of sugar. Rather, the correct expression concerning it is that it is "what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and has not occurred to the heart of any human." If we liken it to foods, we say nonetheless: "Not like these foods." If we liken it to intercourse, we say: "Not like the intercourse known in this world." So how should the wonderers wonder at our saying that the inhabitants of earth and heaven have obtained of God—exalted is He—only attributes and names? And we say: They have obtained of Paradise only attributes and names. Likewise in everything of which a human has heard the name and description, but has not tasted it, apprehended it, reached it, or been characterized by it.

If you say: "Then what is the end of the knowers' knowledge of God—exalted is He?"—I say: The end of the knowers' knowledge is their incapacity for knowledge, and their knowledge in reality that they do not know Him, that they cannot possibly know Him, and that it is impossible for anyone to know God with the true knowledge that encompasses the inner reality of the lordly attributes—except God—mighty and majestic is He. When that is disclosed to them with a demonstrative disclosure, as we have mentioned, then they have known Him—that is, they have reached the utmost limit possible for creatures in knowledge of Him. This is what al-Ṣiddīq al-Akbar, Abū Bakr—may God be pleased with him—pointed to when he said: "The incapacity to attain apprehension is itself apprehension." And it is what the Master of humankind—God's prayers and peace be upon him—meant when he said: "I do not enumerate praise of You; You are as You have praised Yourself." He did not mean that he knew of Him something his tongue could not express; rather, his meaning is: "I do not encompass Your praiseworthy qualities and Your divine attributes; rather, You alone encompass them."

Thus no creature obtains, in contemplating the reality of His Essence, anything but bewilderment (ḥayrah) and astonishment (dahshah). As for the expansion of knowledge, it is in knowledge of His names and attributes.

If you say: "Then by what do the degrees of the angels, prophets, and saints differ in knowledge of Him, if knowledge of Him is not conceivable?"—I say: You have known that knowledge has two ways. One is the true way, and it is blocked—except for God—exalted is He. No creature stirs to attain it and apprehend it but that the glories of majesty (subuḥāt al-jalāl) repel him into bewilderment; and no one stretches forth to contemplate it but that astonishment lowers his gaze.

As for the second way—knowledge of the attributes and names—that is open to creatures, and in it their ranks differ. For one who knows that He—mighty and majestic is He—is knowing and powerful in general is not like one who has witnessed the wonders of His signs in the kingdom of the heavens and the earth, the creation of spirits and bodies, and has surveyed the marvels of the dominion and the rarities of the craftsmanship, delving into detail, exhausting the subtleties of wisdom, completing the refinements of governance, and being characterized by all the angelic attributes that bring near to God—mighty and majestic is He—attaining those attributes by way of being characterized by them. Rather, between them is a vast distance that can scarcely be counted. And in the details of that and its measures, the prophets and saints differ.

This will not reach your understanding except through an example—{«ولله المثل الأعلى»} (And to God belongs the most exalted likeness) — Surah al-Naḥl, verse 60. But you know that a complete, God-fearing scholar, for example like al-Shāfiʿī—may God be pleased with him—is known by the doorkeeper of his house, and is known by al-Muzanī—may God have mercy on him—his student. The doorkeeper knows him as a scholar of the Sacred Law, an author in it, and a guide of God's creatures to it, in general. Al-Muzanī knows him not like the doorkeeper's knowledge, but with a knowledge encompassing the details of his attributes and his sciences. Nay, the scholar who masters ten types of the sciences is not known in reality by his student who has mastered only one type—let alone by his servant who has mastered none of his sciences. Rather, one who has mastered one science has in truth known only its tenth, if he equals him in that science so as not to fall short of him. If he falls short of him, then he does not know in reality what he falls short of, except by name and the illusion of generality—namely, that he knows he knows something beyond what he knows. Likewise, understand the difference of creatures in knowledge of God—exalted is He—according to what is disclosed to them of God's known things, the wonders of His power, and the marvels of His signs in this world and the next, in the dominion (mulk) and the kingdom (malakūt). Their knowledge of God—mighty and majestic is He—increases, and their knowledge approaches the knowledge of the reality of God—exalted is He.

If you say: "If they do not know the reality of the Essence, and its knowledge is impossible, have they then known the names and attributes with a complete, true knowledge?"—We say: Far from it! That too is not known completely and in truth except by God—mighty and majestic is He. For when we know that an essence is knowing, we have known an indeterminate thing whose reality we do not know, but we know that it has the attribute of knowledge. If the attribute of knowledge is known to us in reality, then our knowledge that He is knowing is a complete knowledge of the reality of this attribute; otherwise not. And no one knows the reality of God's knowledge—mighty and majestic is He—except one who has the like of His knowledge; and that is none but Him. So none knows it but Him. Others know it only by likening to their own knowledge, as we adduced in the example of likening to sugar. And God's knowledge—mighty and majestic is He—does not resemble the knowledge of creatures at all; so the creatures' knowledge of Him is not a complete, true knowledge, but an illusory, likening knowledge.

Do not wonder at this, for I say: None knows the sorcerer but the sorcerer himself, or a sorcerer like him or above him. As for one who does not know sorcery and its reality and quiddity, he knows of the sorcerer only his name, and knows that he has a knowledge and a specific property whose nature he does not know—for he does not know its known object, nor does he know what that specific property is. Yes, he knows that that specific property, though indeterminate, is of the genus of sciences, and its fruit is the alteration of hearts, the transformation of the attributes of entities, and the separation between spouses. But this is far removed from knowledge of the reality of sorcery. And one who does not know the reality of sorcery does not know the reality of the sorcerer, because the sorcerer is one who has the specific property of sorcery. The upshot of the name "sorcerer" is that it is a name derived from that attribute: if the attribute is unknown, he is unknown; if it is known, he is known. What is known of sorcery to other than the sorcerer is a general description far from the quiddity—namely, that it is of the genus of sciences, for the name "knowledge" applies to it.

Likewise, what is obtained by us of God's power—mighty and majestic is He—is that it is an attribute whose fruit and effect is the coming-to-be of things, and the name "power" applies to it because it is proportionate to our power with the proportion of the pleasure of intercourse to the pleasure of sugar. And all of this is far removed from the reality of that power. Yes, whenever the servant increases in encompassing the details of the things empowered (maqdūrāt) and the wonders of craftsmanship in the kingdom of the heavens, his share of knowledge of the attribute of power is more abundant—for the fruit indicates the fruit-bearer, just as whenever the student increases in encompassing the details of the teacher's sciences and works, his knowledge of him is more complete and his magnification of him more perfect.

To this reverts the difference of the knowers' knowledge, and there attaches to it a difference that does not terminate. For what the human is unable to know of God's known things has no end, and what he is able to know also has no end—even if what enters into existence from it is finite. But the human's capacity for sciences has no end. Yes, what comes forth into existence differs in abundance and scarcity, and by it the difference appears. It is like the difference among people in the power obtained by wealth: one owns a dāniq and a dirham, another owns thousands. Likewise the sciences—rather, the difference in sciences is greater, because the known things have no end, while the entities of wealth are bodies, and bodies are finite; it is inconceivable that finitude be removed from them.

So you have known how creatures differ in the seas of knowledge of God—mighty and majestic is He—and that this has no end. And you have known that he who says "None knows God but God" has spoken truly, and that he who says "I know none but God" has also spoken truly. For there is nothing in existence but God—mighty and majestic is He—and His acts. If one looks at His acts insofar as they are His acts, confining his gaze to Him, and does not see them insofar as they are sky, earth, and tree, but insofar as they are His handiwork—then he has not passed beyond his knowledge into the presence of lordship, and he may say: "I know none but God, and I see none but God—mighty and majestic is He."

If a person could conceive of seeing nothing but the sun and its light spreading through the horizons, it would be valid for him to say "I see nothing but the sun," for the light flowing from it is part of it, not outside it. And everything in existence is a light from the lights of eternal power and an effect of its effects.

Just as the sun is the spring of the light flowing upon everything illuminated, so the meaning that language fell short of expressing—expressed as "eternal power" out of necessity—is the spring of existence flowing upon everything existent. So there is nothing in existence but God—mighty and majestic is He—and it is permissible for the knower to say: "

### | الفن الثاني في المقاصد والغايات وفي فصول ثلاثة

### | الفصل الأول في شرح معاني أسماء الله التسعة والتسعين

وهي التي اشتملت عليها رواية أبي هريرة رضي الله عنه إذ قال قال رسول صلى
الله عليه وسلم إن لله عز وجل تسعة وتسعين اسما مئة إلا واحدا إنه وتر يحب
الوتر من أحصاها دخل الجنة
هو الله الذي لا إله هو

### | الرحمن الرحيم

الملك القدوس السلام المؤمن المهيمن العزيز الجبار المتكبر الخالق البارئ
المصور الغفار القهار الوهاب الرزاق الفتاح العليم القابض الباسط الخافض
الرافع المعز المذل السميع البصير الحكم العدل اللطيف الخبير الحليم العظيم
الغفور الشكور العلي الكبير الحفيظ المقيت الحسيب الجليل الكريم الرقيب
المجيب الواسع الحكيم الودود المجيد الباعث الشهيد الحق الوكيل القوي
المتين الولي الحميد المحصي المبدئ المعيد المحي المميت الحي القيوم الواجد
الماجد الواحد الصمد القادر المقتدر المقدم المؤخر الأول الآخر الظاهر
الباطن الوالي المتعالي البر التواب المنتقم العفو الرؤوف مالك الملك ذو
الجلال والإكرام المقسط الجامع الغني المغني المانع الضار النافع النور
الهادي البديع الباقي الوارث الرشيد الصبور
فأما قوله الله فهو اسم للموجود الحق الجامع لصفات الإلهية المنعوت بنعوت
الربوبية المتفرد بالوجود الحقيقي فإن كل موجود سواه غير مستحق الوجود
بذاته وإنما استفاد الوجود منه فهو من حيث ذاته هالك ومن الجهة التي تليه
موجود فكل موجود هالك إلا وجهه والأشبه أنه جار في  الدلالة على هذا المعنى
مجرى أسماء الأعلام وكل ما ذكر في اشتقاقه وتعريفه تعسف وتكلف فائدة
اعلم أن هذا الإسم أعظم أسماء الله عز وجل التسعة والتسعين لأنه دال على
الذات الجامعة لصفات الإلهية كلها حتى لا يشذ منها شيء وسائر الأسماء لا
يدل آحادها إلا على آحاد المعاني من علم أو قدرة أو فعل أو غيره ولأنه أخص
الأسماء إذ لا يطلقه أحد على غيره لا حقيقة ولا مجازا وسائر الأسماء قد
يسمى به غيره كالقادر والعليم والرحيم وغيره فلهذين الوجهين يشبه أن يكون
هذا الاسم أعظم هذه الأسماء دقيقة
معاني سائر الأسماء يتصور أن يتصف العبد بشيء منها حتى ينطلق عليه الإسم
كالرحيم والعليم والحليم والصبور والشكور وغيره وإن كان إطلاق الاسم عليه
على وجه آخر يباين إطلاقه على الله عز وجل وأما معنى هذا الاسم فخاص خصوصا
لا يتصور فيه مشاركة لا بالمجاز ولا بالحقيقة ولأجل هذا الخصوص يوصف سائر
الأسماء بأنها اسم الله عز وجل ويعرف بالإضافة إليه فيقال الصبور والشكور
والملك والجبار من أسماء الله عز وجل ولا يقال الله من أسماء الشكور
والصبور لأن ذلك من حيث هو أدل على كنه المعاني الإلهية وأخص بها فكان أشهر
وأظهر فاستغني عن التعريف بغيره وعرف غيره بالإضافة إليه
تنبيه
ينبغي أن يكون حظ العبد من هذا الاسم التأله وأعني به أن يكون مستغرق
القلب والهمة بالله عز وجل لا يرى غيره ولا يلتفت إلى سواه ولا يرجو ولا
يخاف إلا إياه وكيف لا يكون كذلك وقد فهم من هذا الإسم أنه الموجود الحقيقي
الحق وكل ما سواه فان وهالك وباطل إلا به فيرى أولا نفسه أول هالك وباطل
كما رآه رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم حيث قال أصدق بيت قالته العرب قول
لبيد
ألا كل شيء ما خلا الله باطل ... وكل نعيم لا محالة زائل

chapters.anchors:
- Root: أ-ل-ه (aliha)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core sense of worship, devotion, and profound veneration; the object of adoration (maʿbūd) to whom hearts are drawn in awe and love.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The name "Allāh" denotes the Necessary Existent (wājib al-wujūd) Who unites all attributes of divinity (ṣifāt al-ilāhiyyah), being uniquely deserving of worship by virtue of His self-subsistent reality.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage exclusively for God — no metaphorical (majāz) extension to any creature; other divine names permit analogical predication, but this one is absolutely unique.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Proper Noun Specificity (Khuṣūṣiyyat al-ʿAlam) — proper nouns (asmāʾ al-aʿlām) function as direct pointers without derivational mediation; treating "Allāh" as derived (mushtaqq) involves taʿassuf (strained effort), as the author notes.
chapters.translation:
I say: The Second Art concerns aims and purposes, comprising three chapters.

Chapter One: Explaining the meanings of the ninety-nine names of God.

These are the names contained in the narration of Abū Hurayrah (may God be pleased with him), who said: The Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) said: {«Indeed, God — Mighty and Majestic — has ninety-nine names: one hundred minus one. Verily, He is Odd (Watr) and loves the odd. Whoever enumerates them (aḥṣāhā) shall enter Paradise.»} He is God, there is no deity but Him.

The All-Merciful (al-Raḥmān), the Compassionate (al-Raḥīm), the Sovereign (al-Malik), the Holy (al-Quddūs), the Peace (al-Salām), the Faithful (al-Muʾmin), the Guardian (al-Muhaymin), the Mighty (al-ʿAzīz), the Compeller (al-Jabbār), the Proud (al-Mutakabbir), the Creator (al-Khāliq), the Maker (al-Bāriʾ), the Fashioner (al-Muṣawwir), the Forgiving (al-Ghaffār), the Subduer (al-Qahhār), the Bestower (al-Wahhāb), the Provider (al-Razzāq), the Opener (al-Fattāḥ), the All-Knowing (al-ʿAlīm), the Withholder (al-Qābiḍ), the Expander (al-Bāsiṭ), the Abaser (al-Khāfiḍ), the Exalter (al-Rāfiʿ), the Honorer (al-Muʿizz), the Humiliator (al-Mudhill), the All-Hearing (al-Samīʿ), the All-Seeing (al-Baṣīr), the Judge (al-Ḥakam), the Just (al-ʿAdl), the Subtle (al-Laṭīf), the Aware (al-Khabīr), the Forbearing (al-Ḥalīm), the Magnificent (al-ʿAẓīm), the Forgiving (al-Ghafūr), the Thankful (al-Shakūr), the Most High (al-ʿAlī), the Great (al-Kabīr), the Preserver (al-Ḥafīẓ), the Sustainer (al-Muqīt), the Reckoner (al-Ḥasīb), the Majestic (al-Jalīl), the Generous (al-Karīm), the Watchful (al-Raqīb), the Answerer (al-Mujīb), the Vast (al-Wāsiʿ), the Wise (al-Ḥakīm), the Loving (al-Wadūd), the Glorious (al-Majīd), the Resurrector (al-Bāʿith), the Witness (al-Shahīd), the Truth (al-Ḥaqq), the Trustee (al-Wakīl), the Strong (al-Qawī), the Firm (al-Matīn), the Patron (al-Walī), the Praiseworthy (al-Ḥamīd), the Enumerator (al-Muḥṣī), the Originator (al-Mubdiʾ), the Restorer (al-Muʿīd), the Giver of Life (al-Muḥyī), the Taker of Life (al-Mumīt), the Living (al-Ḥayy), the Self-Subsistent (al-Qayyūm), the Finder (al-Wājid), the Glorious (al-Mājid), the One (al-Wāḥid), the Eternal Refuge (al-Ṣamad), the Powerful (al-Qādir), the Omnipotent (al-Muqtadir), the Advancer (al-Muqaddim), the Deferrer (al-Muʾakhkhir), the First (al-Awwal), the Last (al-Ākhir), the Manifest (al-Ẓāhir), the Hidden (al-Bāṭin), the Governor (al-Wālī), the Exalted (al-Mutaʿālī), the Righteous (al-Barr), the Acceptor of Repentance (al-Tawwāb), the Avenger (al-Muntaqim), the Pardoner (al-ʿAfuww), the Kind (al-Raʾūf), the Owner of Sovereignty (Mālik al-Mulk), the Possessor of Majesty and Honor (Dhū al-Jalāl wa al-Ikrām), the Equitable (al-Muqsiṭ), the Gatherer (al-Jāmiʿ), the Self-Sufficient (al-Ghanī), the Enricher (al-Mughnī), the Withholder (al-Māniʿ), the Harmer (al-Ḍārr), the Benefiter (al-Nāfiʿ), the Light (al-Nūr), the Guide (al-Hādī), the Incomparable Originator (al-Badīʿ), the Everlasting (al-Bāqī), the Inheritor (al-Wārith), the Rightly-Guiding (al-Rashīd), the Patient (al-Ṣabūr).

As for His saying "Allāh," it is the name for the True Existent (al-mawjūd al-ḥaqq) Who unites the attributes of divinity (ṣifāt al-ilāhiyyah), being described with the descriptions of lordship (rubūbiyyah), uniquely possessing true existence (al-wujūd al-ḥaqīqī). For every existent other than Him is not deserving of existence in itself; rather, it derives existence from Him. Thus, in respect of its own essence, it is perishing (hālik), and only in the aspect that faces Him is it existent. So everything is perishing except His Face {«kullu shayʾin hālikun illā wajhah»}. The most fitting view is that this name, in its indication of this meaning, runs the course of proper nouns (asmāʾ al-aʿlām); and whatever has been mentioned regarding its derivation (ishtiqāq) and definition is strained effort (taʿassuf) and superfluous.

Know that this name is the greatest of the ninety-nine names of God — Mighty and Majestic — because it indicates the Essence (al-dhāt) that unites all the attributes of divinity, such that nothing of them escapes it. The other names, taken individually, indicate only individual meanings — whether knowledge, power, action, or otherwise. And because it is the most specific of the names, since no one applies it to another — neither literally (ḥaqīqah) nor metaphorically (majāz) — whereas other names may be applied to others, such as "the Powerful" (al-Qādir), "the Knowing" (al-ʿAlīm), "the Merciful" (al-Raḥīm), and so forth. For these two reasons, it is fitting that this name be the greatest of these names in subtlety (dīqqah).

The meanings of the other names admit the possibility that a servant may be described by something of them, such that the name applies to him — like the Merciful (al-Raḥīm), the Knowing (al-ʿAlīm), the Forbearing (al-Ḥalīm), the Patient (al-Ṣabūr), the Thankful (al-Shakūr), and others — even though its application to him is in a different mode that diverges from its application to God — Mighty and Majestic. As for the meaning of this name, it is uniquely specific (khāṣṣ khuṣūṣah) such that no participation is conceivable — neither metaphorically nor literally. For this specificity, the other names are described as being "names of God — Mighty and Majestic," and are defined by their relation to Him: it is said, "The Patient, the Thankful, the Sovereign, and the Compeller are among the names of God — Mighty and Majestic," but it is not said, "Allāh is among the names of the Thankful or the Patient." This is because, in itself, it is more indicative of the inner realities of divine meanings (kunh al-maʿānī al-ilāhiyyah) and more specific to them; hence it is more renowned and manifest, dispensing with definition by another, while others are defined by relation to it.

A Reminder (Tanbīh):
The servant's share of this name should be "theosis" (al-taʾalluh) — by which I mean that his heart and aspiration (himmah) be wholly absorbed in God — Mighty and Majestic — seeing none other than Him, turning not to anything besides Him, hoping in none and fearing none but Him. How could it be otherwise, when he has understood from this name that He is the True Existent (al-mawjūd al-ḥaqq), and everything other than Him is perishing, null, and false (bāṭil) except through Him? Thus, he first sees himself as the foremost of the perishing and null — just as the Messenger of God (peace and blessings be upon him) saw it when he said: "The truest verse spoken by the Arabs is the saying of Labīd:

{«Indeed, everything besides God is false (bāṭil), and every delight inevitably fades away.»}

The All-Merciful (al-Raḥmān), the Compassionate (al-Raḥīm).

chapters.title_en: Section 7: On the Names "The Compassionate" (al-Raḥmān) and "The Merciful" (al-Raḥīm), and "The King" (al-Malik), and "The Holy" (al-Quddūs)
chapters.arabic_text:
اسمان مشتقان من الرحمة والرحمة تستدعي مرحوما ولا مرحوم إلا وهو محتاج
والذي ينقضي بسببه حاجة المحتاج من  غير قصد وإرادة وعناية بالمحتاج لا يسمى
رحيما والذي يريد قضاء حاجة المحتاج ولا يقضيها فإن كان قادرا على قضائها
لم يسم رحيما إذ لو تمت الإرادة لوفى بها وإن كان عاجزا فقد يسمى رحيما
باعتبار ما اعتوره من الرقة ولكنه ناقص وإنما الرحمة التامة إفاضة الخير
على المحتاجين وإرادته لهم عناية بهم والرحمة العامة هي التي تتناول
المستحق وغير المستحق ورحمة الله عز وجل تامة وعامة أما تمامها فمن حيث أنه
أراد قضاء حاجات المحتاجين وقضاها وأما عمومها فمن حيث شمولها المستحق وغير
المستحق وعم الدنيا والآخرة وتناول الضرورات والحاجات والمزايا الخارجة
عنهما فهو الرحيم المطلق حقا دقيقة
الرحمة لا تخلو عن رقة مؤلمة تعتري الرحيم فتحركه إلى قضاء حاجة المرحوم
والرب سبحانه وتعالى منزة عنها فلعلك تظن أن ذلك نقصان في
معنى الرحمة فاعلم أن ذلك كمال وليس بنقصان في معنى الرحمة
أما أنه ليس بنقصان فمن حيث أن كمال الرحمة بكمال ثمرتها ومهما قضيت حاجة
المحتاج بكمالها لم يكن للمرحوم حظ في تألم الراحم وتفجعه وإنما تألم
الراحم لضعف نفسه ونقصانها ولا يزيد ضعفها في غرض المحتاج شيئا بعد أن قضيت
كمال حاجته
وأما أنه كمال في معنى الرحمة فهو أن الرحيم عن رقة وتألم يكاد يقصد
بفعله دفع ألم الرقة عن نفسه فيكون قد نظر لنفسه وسعى في غرض نفسه وذلك
ينقص عن كمال معنى الرحمة بل كمال الرحمة أن يكون نظره إلى المرحوم لأجل
المرحوم لا لأجل الاستراحة من ألم الرقة فائدة
الرحمن أخص من الرحيم ولذلك لا يسمى به غير الله عز وجل
والرحيم قد يطلق على غيره فهو من هذا الوجه قريب من اسم الله تعلى الجاري
مجرى العلم وإن كان هذا مشتقا من الرحمة قطعا ولذلك جمع الله عز وجل بينهما
فقال {قل ادعوا الله أو ادعوا الرحمن أيا ما تدعوا فله الأسماء الحسنى} 17
سورة الإسراء / الآية 110 فيلزم من هذا الوجه ومن حيث منعنا الترادف في
الأسماء المحصاة أن يفرق  بين معنى الاسمين فبالحري أن يكون المفهوم من
الرحمن نوعا من الرحمة هي أبعد من مقدروات العباد وهي ما يتعلق بالسعادة
الأخروية فالرحمن هو العطوف على العباد بالإيجاد أولا وبالهداية إلى
الإيمان وأسباب السعادة ثانيا وبالإسعاد في الآخرة ثالثا والإنعام بالنظر
إلى وجهه الكريم رابعا
تنبيه
حظ العبد من اسم الرحمن أن يرحم عباد الله الغافلين فيصرفهم عن طريق
الغفلة إلى الله عز وجل بالوعظ والنصح بطريق اللطف دون العنف وأن ينظر إلى
العصاة بعين الرحمة لا بعين الإزراء وأن يكون كل معصية تجري في العالم
كمصيبة له في نفسه فلا يألو جهدا في إزالتها بقدر وسعه رحمة لذلك العاصي أن
يتعرض لسخط الله ويستحق البعد من جواره
وحظه من اسم الرحيم أن لا يدع فاقة لمحتاج إلا يسدها بقدر طاقته ولا يترك
فقيرا في جواره وبلده إلا ويقوم بتعهده ودفع فقره إما بماله أو جاهه أو
السعي في حقه بالشفاعة إلى غيره فإن عجز عن جميع ذلك فيعينه بالدعاء وإظهار
الحزن بسبب حاجته رقة عليه وعطفا حتى كأنه مساهم له في ضره وحاجته سؤال
وجوابه
لعلك تقول ما معنى كونه تعالى رحيما وكونه أرحم الراحمين والرحيم لا يرى
مبتلى ومضرورا ومعذبا ومريضا وهو يقدر على إماطة ما بهم إلا ويبادر إلى
إماطته والرب سبحانه وتعالى قادر على كفاية كل بلية ودفع كل فقر وغمة
وإماطة كل مرض وإزالة كل ضرر والدنيا طافحة بالأمراض والمحن والبلايا وهو
قادر على إزالة جميعها وتارك عباده ممتحنين بالرزايا والمحن
فجوابك إن الطفل الصغير قد ترق له أمه فتمنعه عن الحجامة والأب العاقل
يحمله عليها قهرا والجاهل يظن أن الرحيم هي الأم دون الأب والعاقل يعلم أن
إيلام الأب إياه بالحجامة من كمال رحمته وعطفه وتمام شفقته وأن الأم له عدو
في صورة صديق فإن الألم القليل إذا كان سببا للذة الكثيرة لم يكن شرا بل
كان خيرا
والرحيم يريد الخير للمرحوم لا محالة وليس في الوجود شر إلا وفي ضمنه خير
لو رفع  ذلك الشر لبطل الخير الذي في ضمنه وحصل ببطلانه شرا أعظم من الشر
الذي يتضمنه فاليد المتآكلة قطعها شر في الظاهر وفي ضمنه الخير الجزيل وهو
