chapters.anchors:
- Root: ج-ل-ل (j-l-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning of grandeur, elevation, and magnificence; al-jalāl denotes the attribute of majesty and awe-inspiring greatness.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological terms, al-Jalīl refers to the perfection of the divine attributes (ṣifāt), as opposed to al-Kabīr which pertains to the perfection of the essence (dhāt).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage denotes physical elevation and magnitude; metaphorical (majāz) usage transfers this to the ineffable majesty of the divine attributes perceived by the inner vision (baṣīrah).
- Root: ك-ر-م (k-r-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root meaning of nobility, honor, and munificence; al-karam is the quality of being generous and bountiful without expectation of return.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Theologically, al-Karīm is the one whose giving exceeds all hope and whose pardon follows upon power; it is an attribute of absolute perfection.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage applies to the noble vine (karm) due to its beneficial qualities; metaphorical usage elevates it to the divine generosity that transcends all created measures.
- Root: ر-ق-ب (r-q-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root meaning of watching, guarding, and observing; al-raqīb is the vigilant observer who never neglects.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Kalām, al-Raqīb combines knowledge (ʿilm) with perpetual preservation (ḥifẓ), entailing a continuous, unbroken awareness.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage denotes physical surveillance; metaphorical usage denotes the divine watchfulness over the heart's hidden movements.
- Root: ج-و-ب (j-w-b)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root meaning of answering, responding, and replying; al-ijābah is the act of granting a request.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Theologically, al-Mujīb is the one who answers supplication (duʿāʾ) and relieves distress (ḍarūrah), even before the call is made.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage denotes verbal response; metaphorical usage denotes the divine pre-eternal provision of needs before they are articulated.
- Root: و-س-ع (w-s-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Root meaning of breadth, capacity, and expanse; al-wusʿ is the capacity to encompass.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological terms, al-Wāsiʿ denotes the all-encompassing nature of divine knowledge and beneficence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal usage denotes spatial extension; metaphorical usage denotes the boundless scope of divine mercy and cognition.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of ʿAṭf al-Bayān (Appositional Clarification) — When multiple divine names are juxtaposed (e.g., al-Jalīl, al-Jamīl), each functions as an explicative appositive clarifying distinct aspects of the same subject, requiring careful parsing of the genitive construct (iḍāfah) and predicate structure.
chapters.translation:
### | The Majestic (al-Jalīl)

The Absolute belongs solely to God, Mighty and Majestic. Thus, it is as if al-Kabīr (The Great) refers to the perfection of the essence (kamāl al-dhāt), while al-Jalīl (The Majestic) refers to the perfection of the attributes (kamāl al-ṣifāt), and al-ʿAẓīm (The Tremendous) refers to the perfection of both essence and attributes together, relative to the perception of inner vision (baṣīrah) — when it is such that it overwhelms the inner vision, while the inner vision cannot overwhelm it.

Then, the attributes of majesty (ṣifāt al-jalāl), when they are related to the inner vision that perceives them, are called beauty (jamāl), and the one characterized by them is called beautiful (jamīl). The name "beautiful" (al-jamīl) was originally coined for the outward form perceived by the eye (baṣar), whenever it is such that it pleases the eye and harmonizes with it. Then it was transferred (nuqila) to the inward form perceived by the inner visions (baṣāʾir), so that one says "a goodly and beautiful conduct" and "a beautiful character" — and that is perceived by inner visions, not by outward eyes. When the inward form is complete, proportionate, and gathers all its befitting perfections as it ought and in the manner it ought, then it is beautiful in relation to the inner vision that perceives it, harmonizing with it in a harmony whose possessor, upon contemplating it, experiences more delight, joy, and rapture than the beholder with the outward eye experiences toward a beautiful form.

Thus, the True Absolute Beautiful (al-Jamīl al-Ḥaqq al-Muṭlaq) is solely God, Glorified and Exalted — because everything in the world of beauty, perfection, splendor, and comeliness is from the lights of His essence and the traces of His attributes. There is no existent in existence that possesses absolute perfection, devoid of any duality — neither by necessity (wujūban) nor by possibility (imkānan) — other than Him. Therefore, the one who knows Him and contemplates His beauty experiences such delight, joy, pleasure, and bliss that the delights of Paradise and the beauty of visible forms are deemed contemptible in comparison. Indeed, there is no proportion between the beauty of outward forms and the beauty of inward meanings perceived by the inner visions.

We have unveiled this meaning in the Book of Love (Kitāb al-Maḥabbah) from the books of the Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn. Since it is established that He is Majestic (Jalīl) and Beautiful (Jamīl), and every beautiful thing is beloved and cherished by the one who perceives its beauty, therefore God, Mighty and Majestic, is beloved — but among the knowers (ʿārifūn), just as the beautiful outward form is beloved among the seers, not among the blind.

**Admonition (Tanbīh):**
The Majestic and Beautiful among the servants is the one whose inward attributes are good — those which the insightful hearts take delight in. As for outward beauty, its rank is lowly.

### | The Generous (al-Karīm)

He is the one who, when He has power, pardons; when He promises, He fulfills; when He gives, He exceeds the utmost limit of hope. He does not care how much He gives, nor to whom He gives. If a need is raised to other than Him, He is not pleased. When He is treated with aversion, He gently reproaches and does not exact retribution. He does not let perish the one who seeks refuge in Him and clings to Him, and He suffices him without need of means (wasāʾil) or intercessors (shufaʿāʾ). Whoever possesses all of this without affectation (takalluf) — he is the Absolute Generous (al-Karīm al-Muṭlaq), and that is solely for God, Glorified and Exalted.

**Admonition (Tanbīh):**
These traits a servant may adorn himself with in acquiring them, but only in some matters and with a degree of affectation. Therefore, he may be described as

### | The Generous (al-Karīm)

— but he is deficient in relation to the Absolute Generous. And how could the servant not be described by it, when the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: "Do not call the grapevine 'al-karm,' for al-karm is the Muslim man." It was said that the grapevine was described as karm only because its tree is delicate, its fruit is good, its picking is easy, its reach is near, and it is free from thorns and harmful causes — unlike the date-palm.

### | The Watchful (al-Raqīb)

He is the Knowing, the Preserving (al-ʿAlīm al-Ḥafīẓ). Whoever tends to a thing such that he does not neglect it, and observes it with a perpetual, unceasing observation — such that if the one prohibited from it knew of it, he would not venture upon it — is called a watchful one (raqīb). Thus, it is as if it reverts to knowledge and preservation, but in the mode of being perpetual and constant, in relation to that which is prohibited and guarded against being touched.

**Admonition (Tanbīh):**
The description of watchfulness (murāqabah) for the servant is only praiseworthy when his watchfulness is over his Lord and his heart — namely, that he knows that God, Exalted, is his Watcher and Witness in every state, and that he knows that his own soul (nafs) is his enemy, and that Satan is his enemy, and that both of them seize opportunities from him until they carry him into heedlessness (ghaflah) and opposition. Thus, he takes his caution against them by observing their positions, their deceptions, and the places of their incitement, so that he blocks the passages and channels against them. This is his watchfulness.

### | The Responsive (al-Mujīb)

He is the one who answers the requests of the askers with granting (isʿāf), the supplications of the callers with response (ijābah), and the necessities of the distressed with sufficiency (kifāyah). Rather, He bestows favor before the call and grants grace before the supplication. And that is solely for God, Mighty and Exalted — for He knows the need of the needy before their asking, and He knew it in pre-eternity (azal), so He ordained the causes of sufficing needs by creating foods and provisions, and facilitating the means and instruments that lead to all important matters.

**Admonition (Tanbīh):**
The servant ought to be responsive, first, to his Lord, Exalted, in what He has commanded him and forbidden him, and in what He has summoned him to and called him toward; then to His servants, in what God, Mighty and Exalted, has granted him power over, and in granting every asker what he asks if he is able, and in the gentleness of the reply if he is incapable. God, Mighty and Exalted, said: {«وَأَمَّا السَّائِلَ فَلَا تَنْهَرْ»} (As for the petitioner, do not repel him) — Sūrat al-Ḍuḥā, verse 10.

### | 10 —

And the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: "If I were invited to a sheep's hoof, I would accept; and if a sheep's shank were gifted to me, I would accept." His attending of invitations and his acceptance of gifts was the utmost of honoring and responding from him. How many a base, arrogant one elevates himself above accepting any gift and does not humble himself to attend any invitation — rather, he guards his prestige and pride, and does not care about the heart of the asker and inviter, even if he is harmed by his cause. Such a one has no share in the meaning of this name.

### | The Vast (al-Wāsiʿ)

It is derived from vastness (saʿah). Vastness is attributed, at times, to knowledge — when it expands and encompasses numerous known things — and at other times to beneficence (iḥsān) and the spreading of blessings. However it is measured, and upon whatever it descends, then...

chapters.title_en: The All-Encompassing (al-Wāsiʿ), The Wise (al-Ḥakīm), The Affectionate (al-Wadūd), The Glorious (al-Majīd)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الواسع

المطلق هو الله سبحانه وتعالى لأنه إن نظر إلى علمه فلا ساحل لبحر
معلوماته بل تنفد البحار لو كانت مدادا لكلماته وإن نظر إلى إحسانه ونعمه
فلا نهاية لمقدوراته وكل سعة وإن عظمت فتنتهي إلى طرف والذي لا ينتهي إلى
طرف فهو أحق باسم السعة والله سبحانه وتعالى هو الواسع المطلق لأن كل واسع
بالإضافة إلى ما هو أوسع منه ضيق وكل سعة تنتهي إلى طرف فالزيادة عليه
متصورة وما لا نهاية له ولا طرف فلا يتصور عليه زيادة تنبيه
سعة العبد في معارفه وأخلاقه فإن كثرت علومه فهو واسع بقدر سعة علمه وإن
اتسعت أخلاقه حتى لم يضيقها خوف الفقر وغيظ الحسد وغلبة الحرص وسائر الصفات
فهو واسع وكل ذلك فهو إلى نهاية وإنما الواسع الحق هو الله تعالى

### | الحكيم

ذو الحكمة والحكمة عبارة عن معرفة أفضل الأشياء بأفضل العلوم وأجل
الأشياء هو الله سبحانه وقد سبق أنه لا يعرف كنه معرفته غيره فهو الحكيم
الحق لأنه يعلم أجل الأشياء بأجل العلوم إذ أجل العلوم هو العلم الأزلي
الدائم الذي لا يتصور زواله المطابق للمعلوم مطابقة لا يتطرق إليه خفاء ولا
شبهة ولا يتصف بذلك إلا علم الله سبحانه وتعالى وقد يقال لمن يحسن دقائق
الصناعات ويحكمها ويتقن صنعتها حكيم وكمال ذلك أيضا ليس إلا لله تعالى فهو
الحكيم الحق تنبيه
من عرف جميع الأشياء ولم يعرف الله عز وجل لم يستحق أن يسمى حكيما لأنه
لم يعرف أجل الأشياء وأفضلها والحكمة أجل العلوم وجلالة العلم بقدر جلالة
المعلوم ولا أجل من الله عز وجل ومن  عرف الله تعالى فهو حكيم وإن كان ضعيف
الفطنة في سائر العلوم الرسمية كليل اللسان قاصر البيان فيها إلا أن نسبة
حكمة العبد إلى حكمة الله تعالى كنسبة معرفته به إلى معرفته بذاته وشتان
بين المعرفتين فشتان بين الحكمتين ولكنه مع بعده عنه فهو أنفس المعارف
وأكثرها خيرا ومن أوتي الحكمة فقد أوتي خيرا كثيرا
نعم من عرف الله كان كلامه مخالفا لكلام غيره فإنه قلما يتعرض للجزئيات
بل يكون كلامه كليا ولا يتعرض لمصالح العاجلة بل يتعرض لما ينفع في العاقبة
ولما كان ذلك أظهر عند الناس من أحوال الحكيم من معرفته بالله عز وجل ربما
أطلق الناس اسم الحكمة على مثل تلك الكلمات الكلية
ويقال للناطق بها حكيم
وذلك مثل قول سيد البشر صلاة الرحمن وسلامه عليه رأس الحكمة مخافة الله
وقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم الكيس من دان نفسه وعمل لما بعد الموت والعاجز من
أتبع نفسه هواها وتمنى على الله وقوله عليه الصلاة والسلام ما قل وكفى خيرا
مما كثر وألهى وقوله صلى الله عليه وسلم من أصبح معافى في بدنه آمنا في
سربه عنده قوت يومه فكأنما حيزت له الدنيا بحذافيرها وقوله عليه أفضل
الصلاة كن ورعا تكن أعبد الناس وكن قنعا تكن أشكر الناس وقوله البلاء موكل
بالمنطق وقوله من حسن إسلام المرء تركه ما لا يعنيه وقوله السعيد من وعظ
بغيره وقوله الصمت حكمة وقليل فاعله وقوله القناعة مال لا ينفد وقوله الصبر
نصف الإيمان واليقين الإيمان كله فهذه
الكلمات وأمثالها تسمى حكمة وصاحبها يسمى حكيما

### | الودود

هو الذي يحب الخير لجميع الخلق فيحسن إليهم ويثني عليهم وهو قريب من معنى
الرحيم لكن الرحمة إضافة إلى مرحوم والمرحوم هو المحتاج والمضطر وأفعال
الرحيم تستدعي مرحوما ضعيفا وأفعال الودود لا تستدعي ذلك بل الإنعام على
سبيل الابتداء من نتائج الود وكما أن معنى رحمته سبحانه وتعالى إرادته
الخير للمرحوم وكفايته له وهو منزه عن رقة الرحمة فكذلك وده إرادته الكرامة
والنعمة وإحسانه وإنعامه وهو  منزه عن ميل المودة والرحمة لكن المودة
والرحمة لا تراد في حق المرحوم والمودود إلا لثمرتهما وفائدتهما لا للرقة
والميل فالفائدة هي لباب الرحمة والمودة وروحهما وذلك هو المتصور في حق
الله سبحانه وتعالى دون ما هو مقارن لهما وغير مشروط في الإفادة تنبيه
الودود من عباد الله من يريد لخلق الله كل ما يريده لنفسه وأعلى من ذلك
من يؤثرهم على نفسه كمن قال منهم أريد أن أكون جسرا على النار يعبر علي
الخلق ولا يتأذون بها وكمال ذلك أن لا يمنعه عن الإيثار والإحسان الغضب
والحقد وما ناله من الأذى كما قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم حيث كسرت
رباعيته وأدمي وجهه وضرب اللهم اغفر لقومي فإنهم لا يعلمون فلم يمنعه سوء
صنيعهم عن إرادته الخير لهم وكما أمر صلى الله عليه وسلم عليا رضي الله عنه
حيث
قال إن أردت أن تسبق المقربين فصل من قطعك وأعط من حرمك واعف عمن ظلمك

### | المجيد

هو الشريف ذاته الجميل أفعاله الجزيل عطاؤه ونوله فكأن شرف الذات إذا
قارنه حسن الفعال سمي مجدا وهو الماجد أيضا ولكن أحدهما أدل على المبالغة
وكأنه يجمع معاني اسم الجليل والوهاب والكريم وقد سبق الكلام فيها
chapters.anchors:
- Root: و س ع (w-s-ʿ)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Breadth, capacity, amplitude; the opposite of constriction (ḍīq); to embrace, contain, or extend without bound.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine infinitude of knowledge and power; God's encompassing all things in mercy and cognizance, as in {«وَسِعَ كُرْسِيُّهُ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ»}.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for spatial/quantitative extension; metaphorical (majāz) for God as that which no limit terminates, transcending all finite measure.
- Root: ح ك م (ḥ-k-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To prevent, restrain, judge; mastery that issues in perfected action; firmness in speech and deed.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Knowledge of the noblest things by the noblest sciences; the highest wisdom (ḥikmah) is knowledge of God, the most excellent object of cognition.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for sound judgment and craftsmanship; transferred to the wise man whose speech is universal (kullī) and oriented to the afterlife, not particulars of this world.
- Root: و د د (w-d-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Love, affection, yearning for union; the core (lubāb) of a thing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): God's volition to bestow honor and grace upon creatures, devoid of any passional inclination (mayl) or tenderness (riqqah); the fruit and benefit of love, not its bodily concomitants.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for human affection with emotional yearning; metaphorical for God's pure beneficent will, since only the benefit (fāʾidah) is intended, not the sentiment.
- Root: م ج د (m-j-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Glory, honor, nobility of essence; ampleness of giving.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The conjunction of noble essence (sharaf al-dhāt) with beautiful acts (ḥusn al-fiʿāl); a name compounding majesty and munificence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for human nobility; metaphorical for God as the absolute Majīd whose essence is inherently noble and whose acts are inherently perfect.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taḍmīn (Semantic Inclusion) — A verb or noun may carry the sense of another root without its lexical form, as here "sعة" (breadth) implies "encompassing" (iḥāṭah), and "ود" (love) implies "volition" (irādah) in divine predication, requiring the interpreter to extract the intended meaning from the syntactic context of attribution.
chapters.translation:
### | The All-Encompassing (al-Wāsiʿ)

The absolute [possessor of this name] is God, exalted and transcendent, for if one looks to His knowledge, there is no shore to the sea of His known things; rather, the seas would be exhausted were they ink for His words. And if one looks to His beneficence and His graces, there is no end to His objects of power. Every expanse, however great, terminates at a limit, and that which does not terminate at a limit is more worthy of the name "expanse." God, exalted and transcendent, is the absolute All-Encompassing, because every expansive thing, in relation to what is more expansive than it, is constricted; and every expanse that terminates at a limit admits of the conception of increase upon it. But that which has no end and no limit admits of no increase upon it.

**Admonition:** The servant's expanse lies in his cognitions and his moral traits. If his sciences multiply, he is expansive to the measure of his knowledge; and if his character broadens until neither fear of poverty, nor the rage of envy, nor the dominance of greed, nor the rest of the vices constricts it, then he is expansive. Yet all of that terminates at an end. The truly expansive one is only God, exalted.

### | The Wise (al-Ḥakīm)

He is the possessor of wisdom (ḥikmah), and wisdom is the knowledge of the most excellent things by the most excellent sciences. The most august of things is God, exalted — and it has preceded that none knows the reality of His knowledge save He. Thus He is the truly Wise, because He knows the most august of things by the most august of sciences, since the most august of sciences is the eternal, everlasting knowledge that admits of no passing away, conforming to the known object with a conformity that no obscurity or doubt can penetrate. Nothing is described by that save the knowledge of God, exalted and transcendent. And one who perfects the subtleties of crafts, masters them, and executes them with precision may be called "wise" (ḥakīm); yet the perfection of that too belongs only to God, exalted. He is the truly Wise.

**Admonition:** Whoever knows all things but does not know God, mighty and majestic, does not deserve to be called wise, because he has not known the most august and most excellent of things. Wisdom is the most august of sciences, and the dignity of knowledge is proportionate to the dignity of the known object — and there is nothing more august than God, mighty and majestic. Whoever knows God, exalted, is wise, even if he be weak in acumen regarding the other conventional sciences, dull of tongue, and deficient in expression concerning them — except that the ratio of the servant's wisdom to God's wisdom is like the ratio of his knowledge of Him to His knowledge of His own essence. How vast the distance between the two knowledges! So how vast the distance between the two wisdoms! Yet despite its remoteness from Him, it is the most precious of cognitions and the most abundant in good. {«وَمَن يُؤْتَ الْحِكْمَةَ فَقَدْ أُوتِيَ خَيْرًا كَثِيرًا»} — "And whoever is given wisdom has been given abundant good."

Indeed, whoever knows God, his speech differs from the speech of others: he rarely engages with particulars, but rather his speech is universal (kullī); he does not address the interests of the immediate world, but rather addresses what benefits in the final outcome. And since this is more manifest to people than the wise man's knowledge of God, mighty and majestic, people may apply the name "wisdom" to such universal utterances, and the one who utters them is called "wise."

Such are the sayings of the master of mankind — may the prayer of the All-Merciful and His peace be upon him: "The head of wisdom is the fear of God" (رأس الحكمة مخافة الله). And his saying, peace and blessings upon him: "The shrewd one is he who holds his soul to account and works for what comes after death; the incapable one is he who follows his soul's whims and harbors wishes upon God" (الكيس من دان نفسه وعمل لما بعد الموت والعاجز من أتبع نفسه هواها وتمنى على الله). And his saying, peace and blessings upon him: "What is little and suffices is better than what is much and distracts" (ما قل وكفى خيرا مما كثر وألهى). And his saying, peace and blessings upon him: "Whoever wakes up sound in body, secure in his community, having his day's provision — it is as though the world in its entirety were gathered for him" (من أصبح معافى في بدنه آمنا في سربه عنده قوت يومه فكأنما حيزت له الدنيا بحذافيرها). And his saying, upon him the most excellent prayer: "Be scrupulous (warʿ), and you will be the most worshipful of people; be content (qanūʿ), and you will be the most thankful of people" (كن ورعا تكن أعبد الناس وكن قنعا تكن أشكر الناس). And his saying: "Affliction is delegated to speech" (البلاء موكل بالمنطق). And his saying: "Part of the excellence of one's Islam is leaving what does not concern him" (من حسن إسلام المرء تركه ما لا يعنيه). And his saying: "Fortunate is he who is admonished by others" (السعيد من وعظ بغيره). And his saying: "Silence is wisdom, and few practice it" (الصمت حكمة وقليل فاعله). And his saying: "Contentment is wealth that never exhausts" (القناعة مال لا ينفد). And his saying: "Patience is half of faith, and certainty is all of faith" (الصبر نصف الإيمان واليقين الإيمان كله). These words and their like are called wisdom, and their utterer is called wise.

### | The Affectionate (al-Wadūd)

He is the one who loves good for all creatures, so He does good to them and praises them. This is close in meaning to the All-Merciful (al-Raḥīm), except that mercy is a relation to an object of mercy (marḥūm), and the object of mercy is the needy and the constrained. The acts of the All-Merciful require a weak object of mercy, whereas the acts of the Affectionate do not require that; rather, bestowing grace in the manner of initiation (ibtidāʾ) is among the results of affection (wudd). And just as the meaning of His mercy, exalted and transcendent, is His willing good for the object of mercy and His sufficing him — He being exalted above any tenderness of compassion (riqqat al-raḥmah) — so likewise His affection is His willing honor and grace, His beneficence and His bestowal — He being exalted above any inclination of fondness (mayl al-mawaddah) and mercy. But fondness and mercy are not sought with respect to the object of mercy and the object of affection except for their fruit and benefit, not for tenderness and inclination. The benefit is the pith (lubāb) of mercy and affection and their spirit; and that is what is conceivable with respect to God, exalted and transcendent — not what is concomitant with them and not a condition for their efficacy.

**Admonition:** The affectionate one among God's servants is he who wills for God's creatures everything he wills for himself. Higher than that is he who prefers them over himself, like the one among them who said: "I wish to be a bridge over the Fire upon which the creatures cross and are not pained by it." The perfection of that is that neither anger, nor rancor, nor the harm he has suffered should prevent him from preferring others and doing good — as the Messenger of God, peace and blessings upon him, said when his front tooth was broken, his face bloodied, and he was struck: "O God, forgive my people, for they do not know" (اللهم اغفر لقومي فإنهم لا يعلمون). Their evil conduct did not prevent him from willing good for them. And as he, peace and blessings upon him, commanded ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him, when he said: "If you wish to outstrip the near-stationed (muqarrabūn), then join the one who cuts you off, give to the one who deprives you, and forgive the one who wrongs you" (إن أردت أن تسبق المقربين فصل من قطعك وأعط من حرمك واعف عمن ظلمك).

### | The Glorious (al-Majīd)

He is the one noble in essence, beautiful in acts, abundant in giving and bestowal. It is as though when nobility of essence is conjoined with excellence of deed, it is called glory (majd). He is also the Majādid (the Most Glorious), but one of the two forms is more indicative of intensification. It is as though this name combines the meanings of the August (al-Jalīl), the Munificent (al-Wahhāb), and the Generous (al-Karīm) — and the discussion of these has already preceded.

chapters.title_en: The Resurrector (al-Bāʿith) and The Witness (al-Shahīd)
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الباعث

هو الذي يحيي الخلق يوم النشور ويبعث من في القبور ويحصل ما في الصدور
والبعث هو النشأة الآخرة ومعرفة هذا الاسم موقوفة على معرفة حقيقة البعث
وذلك من أغمض المعارف وأكثر الخلق منه على توهمات مجملة وتخيلات مبهمة
وغايتهم فيه تخيلهم أن الموت عدم والبعث إيجاد مبتدأ بعد عدم مثل الإيجاد
الأول فظنهم أن الموت عدم غلط وظنهم أن الإيجاد الثاني مثل الإيجاد الأول
غلط
فأما ظنهم أن الموت عدم فهو باطل بل القبر إما حفرة من حفر النيران أو
روضة من رياض الجنة والميت إما من السعداء وأولئك ليسوا أمواتا بل أحياء
عند ربهم يرزقون فرحين بما آتاهم الله من فضله 3 سورة آل عمران الآية 169 و
170 وإما من الأشقياء وهم أيضا أحياء  ولذلك ناداهم رسول الله صلى الله عليه
وسلم في وقعة بدر وقال إني وجدت ما وعدني ربي
حقا فهل وجدتم ما وعد ربكم حقا ثم لما قيل له كيف تنادي قوما قد جيفوا
قال ما أنتم بأسمع لما أقول منهم لكنهم لا يقدرون أن يجيبوا والمشاهدة
الباطنة دلت أرباب البصائر على أن الإنسان خلق للأبد وأنه لا سبيل عليه
للعدم نعم تارة يقطع تصرفه عن الجسد فيقال مات وتارة يعاد إليه فيقال أحيي
وبعث أي أحيي جسده وكشف ذلك بالحقيقة مما لا يحتمله هذا الكتاب
وأما ظنهم أن البعث ليس إيجادا ثانيا وهو مثل الإيجاد الأول فغير صحيح بل
البعث إنشاء آخر لا يناسب الإنشاء الأول أصلا وللإنسان نشآت كثيرة وليست هي
نشأتين فقط ولذلك قال تعالى وننشئكم فيما لا تعلمون 56 سورة الواقعة الآية
61 ولذلك قال بعد خلق المضغة والعلقة وغير ذلك ثم أنشأناه خلقا آخر فتبارك
الله أحسن الخالقين 23 سورة المؤمنين الآية 14 بل النطفة نشأة من التراب
والعلقة نشأة من النطفة والمضغة نشأة من العلقة والروح نشأة من المضغة
ولشرف نشأة الروح وجلالته وكونه أمرا ربانيا قال عند ذلك ثم أنشأناه خلقا
آخر فتبارك الله أحسن الخالقين 23 سورة المؤمنون الآية 14 وقال تعالى
ويسألونك عن الروح قل الروح من أمر ربي 17 سورة الإسراء الآية 85 ثم خلق
الإدراكات الحسية بعد خلق أصل الروح نشأة أخرى ثم خلق التمييز الذي يظهر
بعد سبع سنين نشأة أخرى ثم خلق العقل بعد خمس عشرة سنة وما يقاربها نشأة
أخرى وكل نشأة طور وقد خلقكم أطوارا 71 سورة نوح الآية 14 ثم ظهور خاصية
الولاية لمن رزق تلك الخاصية نشأة أخرى ثم ظهور خاصية النبوة بعد نشأة أخرى
وهي
نوع من العبث والله سبحانه وتعالى باعث الرسل كما أنه الباعث يوم النشور
وكما أنه يعسر على ابن المهد فهم حقيقة التمييز قبل حصول التمييز ويعسر
على المميز فهم حقيقة العقل وما ينكشف في طوره من العجائب قبل  حصول العقل
فكذلك يعسر فهم طور الولاية والنبوة في طور العقل فإن الولاية طور كمال
وراء نشأة العقل كما أن العقل طور كمال وراء نشأة التمييز والتمييز طور
كمال وراء نشأة الحواس وكما أن من طباع الناس إنكار ما لم يبلغوه ولم
ينالوه حتى إن كل واحد ينكر ما لم يشاهده ولم يحصل له ولا يؤمن بما غاب عنه
فمن طباعهم إنكار الولاية وعجائبها والنبوة وغرائبها بل من طباعهم إنكار
النشأة الثانية والحياة الآخرة لأنهم لم يبلغوها بعد ولو عرض طور العقل
وعالمه وما يظهر فيه من العجائب على المميز لأنكره وجحده وأحال وجوده فمن
آمن بشيء مما لم يبلغه فقد آمن بالغيب وذلك هو مفتاح السعادات
وكما أن طور العقل وإدراكاته ونشأته بعيد المناسبة عن الإدراكات التي
قبله فكذلك النشأة الآخرة بل أبعد فلا ينبغي أن تقاس النشأة الآخرة بالأولى
وهذه النشآت هي أطوار ذات واحدة ومراقيها التي تصعد فيها إلى درجات الكمال
حتى تقرب من الحضرة التي هي منتهى كل كمال وتكون عند الله عز وجل بين رد
وقبول وحجاب ووصول فإن قبل رقي إلى أعلى العليين وإلا رد إلى أسفل السافلين
والمقصود أن لا مناسبة بين النشأتين إلا من حيث الاسم ومن لم يعرف النشأة
والبعث لم يعرف معنى اسم الباعث وشرح ذلك يطول فلنتجاوزه
تنبيه
حقيقة البعث ترجع إلى إحياء الموتى بإنشائهم نشأة أخرى والجهل هو الموت
الأكبر والعلم هو الحياة الأشرف وقد ذكر الله سبحانه وتعالى العلم والجهل
في كتابه العزيز وسماهما حياة وموتا ومن رقى غيره من الجهل إلى المعرفة فقد
أنشأه نشأة أخرى وأحياه حياة طيبة فإن كان للعبد مدخل في إفادة الخلق العلم
ودعائهم إلى الله تعالى فذلك نوع من الإحياء وهي رتبة الأنبياء ومن يرثهم
من العلماء

### | الشهيد

يرجع معناه إلى العليم مع خصوص إضافة فإن الله عز وجل عالم الغيب
والشهادة والغيب عبارة عما بطن والشهادة عما ظهر وهو الذي يشاهد فإذا اعتبر
العلم مطلقا فهو العليم وإذا أضيف إلى  الغيب والأمور الباطنة فهو الخبير
وإذا أضيف إلى الأمور الظاهرة فهو الشهيد وقد يعتبر مع هذا أن يشهد على
الخلق يوم القيامة بما علم وشاهد منهم والكلام في هذا الاسم يقرب من الكلام
في العليم والخبير فلا نعيده

- Root: ب ع ث (b-ʿ-th)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To rouse, raise up, send forth; the core sense is an abrupt arousal from a state of quiescence or dissolution, whether from sleep, death, or a prior condition of non-manifestation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In Qur'anic usage, al-baʿth is the eschatological re-creation and re-embodiment of the dead for judgment; it is an act of divine origination (inshāʾ) that is categorically distinct from the first creation, not a mere repetition.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) for physical resurrection; metaphorical (majāz) for spiritual elevation from ignorance to knowledge, as when one "raises" another from the grave of ignorance.
- Root: ش ه د (sh-h-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To be present, to witness, to testify; the root implies direct presence and ocular or intellectual apprehension, as opposed to absence (ghayb).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): al-Shahīd is the One whose knowledge encompasses all manifest things (al-shahādah) in a mode of immediate presence, and who will bear witness against creation on the Day of Judgment.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for sensory presence; metaphorical for God's eternal knowledge of the apparent, since He is never absent from any state.
- Sībawayh Rule: The Rule of Complementarity (al-Taqābul) — the pairing of al-Bāʿith with al-Shahīd in this section follows the syntactic pattern of contrasting opposites (death/life, hidden/apparent) to establish a complete semantic field, as in the nominal sentence structure "al-ghayb ʿibāratun ʿammā baṭana" (the hidden is an expression of what is concealed).
chapters.translation:
### | The Resurrector (al-Bāʿith)

He is the One who gives life to creation on the Day of Arising (al-nushūr), raises up those who are in the graves, and brings to pass what is in the breasts.

Now, "resurrection" (al-baʿth) is the second origination (al-nashʾah al-ākhirah), and knowledge of this name is contingent upon knowledge of the true reality of resurrection. And this is among the most obscure of cognitions; most of creation holds only vague suppositions and obscure fancies regarding it. Their ultimate reach in this matter is the fancy that death is non-existence (ʿadam) and that resurrection is an origination ex nihilo after non-existence, like the first origination. Thus their supposition that death is non-existence is an error, and their supposition that the second origination is like the first origination is an error.

As for their supposition that death is non-existence, it is false. Rather, the grave is either a pit of the pits of the Fire or a meadow of the meadows of Paradise. The dead person is either among the blessed — and those are not dead, but alive with their Lord, provided for, rejoicing in what God has given them of His bounty {«فَرِحِينَ بِمَا آتَاهُمُ اللَّهُ مِنْ فَضْلِهِ»} (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān, 3:169–170) — or among the wretched, and they too are alive. For this reason, the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, called out to them at the Battle of Badr and said: "I have found what my Lord promised me to be true; have you found what your Lord promised you to be true?" Then when it was said to him, "How do you call out to a people whose bodies have already putrefied?" he said: "You are not more hearing of what I say than they are, but they are unable to answer." And inner witnessing (al-mushāhadah al-bāṭinah) has indicated to the people of insight that the human being was created for eternity (al-abad) and that non-existence has no path over him. Yes, at times his disposal (taṣarruf) is cut off from the body, and it is said "he died"; and at times it is restored to it, and it is said "he was given life" and "he was raised" — that is, his body was given life. The unveiling of this in its true reality is not something this book can bear.

As for their supposition that resurrection is not a second origination but is like the first origination, this is not sound. Rather, resurrection is another origination (inshāʾ ākhar) that bears no proportion (munāsabah) whatsoever to the first origination. The human being has many origination-stages (nashʾāt), not merely two. For this reason, the Exalted said: {«وَنُنْشِئَكُمْ فِي مَا لَا تَعْلَمُونَ»} (Sūrat al-Wāqiʿah, 56:61). And for this reason He said, after the creation of the embryo-clot (al-muḍghah), the clinging-drop (al-ʿalaqah), and other stages: {«ثُمَّ أَنْشَأْنَاهُ خَلْقًا آخَرَ فَتَبَارَكَ اللَّهُ أَحْسَنُ الْخَالِقِينَ»} (Sūrat al-Muʾminūn, 23:14). Rather, the drop of sperm (al-nuṭfah) is an origination from dust; the clinging-drop is an origination from the sperm-drop; the embryo-clot is an origination from the clinging-drop; and the spirit (al-rūḥ) is an origination from the embryo-clot. And because of the nobility and majesty of the origination of the spirit, and its being a lordly command (amr rabbānī), He said at that point: {«ثُمَّ أَنْشَأْنَاهُ خَلْقًا آخَرَ فَتَبَارَكَ اللَّهُ أَحْسَنُ الْخَالِقِينَ»} (Sūrat al-Muʾminūn, 23:14). And the Exalted said: {«وَيَسْأَلُونَكَ عَنِ الرُّوحِ قُلِ الرُّوحُ مِنْ أَمْرِ رَبِّي»} (Sūrat al-Isrāʾ, 17:85). Then the creation of the sensory perceptions (al-idrākāt al-ḥissiyyah) after the creation of the root of the spirit is another origination. Then the creation of discernment (al-tamyīz), which appears after seven years, is another origination. Then the creation of the intellect (al-ʿaql) after fifteen years or thereabouts is another origination. And every origination is a stage (ṭawr), for He said: {«وَقَدْ خَلَقَكُمْ أَطْوَارًا»} (Sūrat Nūḥ, 71:14). Then the appearance of the specific property of sainthood (al-wilāyah) for one who is granted that property is another origination. Then the appearance of the specific property of prophethood (al-nubuwwah) is yet another origination.

And it is a kind of futility (ʿabath) [to deny what one has not reached]. For God, glorified and exalted, is the Sender of the messengers (bāʿith al-rusul) just as He is the Resurrector on the Day of Arising. And just as it is difficult for the child to understand the reality of discernment before discernment is attained, and difficult for the one who discerns to understand the reality of the intellect and the wonders disclosed in its stage before the intellect is attained, so too is it difficult to understand the stage of sainthood and prophethood while in the stage of the intellect. For sainthood is a stage of perfection beyond the origination of the intellect, just as the intellect is a stage of perfection beyond the origination of discernment, and discernment is a stage of perfection beyond the origination of the senses. And just as it is the nature of people to deny what they have not reached and attained — indeed, every person denies what he has not witnessed and not obtained, and does not believe in what is absent from him — so it is their nature to deny sainthood and its wonders, and prophethood and its marvels. Nay, it is their nature to deny the second origination and the afterlife, because they have not yet reached it. And if the stage of the intellect and its world and the wonders appearing in it were presented to one who only discerns, he would deny it, reject it, and deem its existence impossible. So whoever believes in something he has not yet reached has believed in the unseen (al-ghayb), and that is the key to felicities (miftāḥ al-saʿādāt).

And just as the stage of the intellect, its perceptions, and its origination are far in proportion (baʿīd al-munāsabah) from the perceptions that precede it, so too is the final origination — nay, even farther. Therefore, the final origination should not be measured against the first. These origination-stages are stages (aṭwār) of a single essence (dhāt wāḥidah) and its ascents (marāqī) by which it ascends to degrees of perfection, until it draws near to the Presence (al-ḥaḍrah) that is the terminus of every perfection. And it is with God, mighty and majestic, between rejection and acceptance, and between veil and arrival. If it is accepted, it ascends to the Highest of the High (ʿilliyyīn); otherwise, it is cast down to the Lowest of the Low (asfal sāfilīn).

The point is that there is no proportion between the two origination-stages except in name. And whoever does not know the origination and the resurrection does not know the meaning of the name "The Resurrector." The elaboration of this would be lengthy, so let us pass over it.

**A Reminder (Tanbīh):**

The reality of resurrection reduces to the giving of life to the dead by originating them in another origination. And ignorance (al-jahl) is the greater death, while knowledge (al-ʿilm) is the nobler life. God, glorified and exalted, has mentioned knowledge and ignorance in His Mighty Book and called them life and death. And whoever raises another from ignorance to knowledge has originated him in another origination and given him a goodly life (ḥayāh ṭayyibah). For if a servant has a share in benefiting creation with knowledge and calling them to God, exalted, that is a kind of giving life — and that is the rank of the prophets and of the scholars who inherit from them.

### | The Witness (al-Shahīd)

Its meaning reverts to "The Knowing" (al-ʿAlīm) with a specific addition (khuṣūṣ iḍāfah). For God, mighty and majestic, is the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed (ʿālim al-ghayb wa-al-shahādah). The unseen (al-ghayb) is an expression for what is hidden, and the witnessed (al-shahādah) for what is apparent. And He is the One who witnesses (yushāhid). So if knowledge is considered absolutely, He is "The Knowing" (al-ʿAlīm). If it is added to the unseen and hidden matters, He is "The Aware" (al-Khabīr). And if it is added to apparent matters, He is "The Witness" (al-Shahīd). It may also be considered, along with this, that He bears witness against creation on the Day of Resurrection regarding what He knew and witnessed from them. The discussion of this name is close to the discussion of "The Knowing" and "The Aware," so we shall not repeat it.

### | الحق

هو في مقابلة الباطل والأشياء قد تستبان بأضدادها وكل ما يخبر عنه فإما
باطل مطلقا وإما حق مطلقا وإما حق من وجه باطل من وجه فالممتنع بذاته هو
الباطل مطلقا والواجب بذاته هو الحق مطلقا والممكن بذاته الواجب بغيره هو
حق من وجه باطل من وجه فهو من حيث ذاته لا وجود له فهو باطل وهو من جهة
غيره مستفيد للوجود فهو من هذا الوجه الذي يلي مفيد الوجود موجود فهو من
ذلك الوجه حق ومن جهة نفسه باطل فلذلك قال تعالى كل شيء هالك إلا وجهه 28
سورة
القصص الآية 88 وهو كذلك أزلا وأبدا ليس ذلك في حال دون حال لأن كل شيء
سواه أزلا وأبدا من حيث ذاته لا يستحق الوجود ومن جهته يستحق فهو باطل
بذاته حق بغيره وعند هذا تعرف أن الحق المطلق هو الموجود الحقيقي بذاته
الذي منه يأخذ كل حق حقيقته
وقد يقال أيضا للمعقول الذي صادف به العقل الموجود حتى طابقه إنه حق فهو
من حيث ذاته يسمى موجودا ومن حيث إضافته إلى العقل الذي أدركه على ما هو
عليه يسمى حقا فإذا أحق الموجودات بأن يكون حقا هو الله تعالى وأحق المعارف
بأن تكون حقا هيمعرفة الله عز وجل فإنه حق في نفسه أي مطابق للمعلوم أزلا
وأبدا ومطابقته لذاته لا لغيره لا كالعلم بوجود غيره فإنه لا يكون إلا ما
دام ذلك الغير موجودا فإذا عدم عاد ذلك الاعتقاد باطلا وذلك الاعتقاد أيضا
لا يكون حقا لذات المعتقد لأنه ليس موجودا لذاته بل هو موجود لغيره
وقد يطلق ذلك على الأقوال فيقال قول حق وقول باطل وعلى ذلك فأحق الأقوال
قولك لا إله إلا الله لأنه صادق أبدا وأزلا لذاته لا  لغيره
فإذا يطلق الحق على الوجود في الأعيان وعلى الوجود في الأذهان وهو
المعرفة وعلى الوجود الذي في اللسان وهو النطق فأحق الأشياء بأن يكون حقا
هو الذي يكون وجوده ثابتا لذاته أزلا وأبدا ومعرفته حقا أزلا وأبدا
والشهادة له حقا أزلا وأبدا وكل ذلك لذات الموجود الحقيقي لا لغيره تنبيه
حظ العبد من هذا الاسم أن يرى نفسه باطلا ولا يرى غير الله عز
وجل حقا والعبد إن كان حقا فليس حقا بنفسه بل هو حق بالله عز وجل فإنه
موجود به لا بذاته بل هو بذاته باطل لولا إيجاد الحق له فقد أخطأ من قال
أنا الحق إلا بأحد التأويلين
أحدهما أن يعني أنه بالحق وهذا التأويل بعيد لأن اللفظ لا ينبىء عنه ولأن
ذلك لا يخصه بل كل شيء سوى الحق فهو بالحق
التأويل الثاني أن يكون مستغرقا بالحق حتى لا يكون فيه متسع لغيره وما
أخذ كلية الشيء واستغرقه فقد يقال إنه هو كما يقول الشاعر
أنا من أهوى ومن أهوى أنا ... نحن روحان حللنا بدنا
ويعني به الاستغراق
وأهل التصوف لما كان الغالب عليهم رؤية فناء أنفسهم من حيث ذاتهم كان
الجاري على لسانهم من أسماء الله تعالى وفي أكثر الأقوال والأحوال هو الحق
لأنهم يلحظون الذات الحقيقية دون ما هو هالك في نفسه
وأهل الكلام لما كانوا أبعد في مقام الاستدلال بالأفعال كان الجاري على
لسانهم في الأكثر اسم البارئ الذي هو بمعنى الخالق
وأكثر الخلق يرون كل شيء سواه فيستشهدون عليه بما يرونه وهم المخاطبون
بقوله تعالى أولم ينظروا في ملكوت السموات والأرض وما خلق الله من شيء 7
سورة الأعراف الآية 185
والصديقون لا يرون شيئا سواه فيستشهدون به عليه وهم المخاطبون بقوله
تعالى أولم يكف بربك أنه على كل شيء شهيد 41 سورة فصلت الآية 53

### | الوكيل

هو الموكول إليه الأمور ولكن الموكول إليه ينقسم إلى من يوكل إليه بعض
الأمور وذلك ناقص وإلى من يوكل إليه الكل وليس ذلك إلا  الله سبحانه وتعالى
والموكول إليه ينقسم إلى من يستحق أن يكون موكولا إليه لا بذاته ولكن
بالتفويض والتوكيل وهذا ناقص لأنه فقير إلى التفويض والتولية وإلى من يستحق
بذاته أن تكون الأمور موكولة إليه والقلوب متوكلة عليه لا بتولية وتفويض من
جهة غيره وذلك هو الوكيل المطلق والوكيل أيضا ينقسم إلى من يفي بما وكل
إليه وفاء تاما من غير قصور وإلى من لا يفي بالجميع والوكيل المطلق هو الذي
الأمور موكولة إليه وهو ملي بالقيام بها وفي بإتمامها وذلك هو الله تعالى
فقط وقد فهمت من هذا مقدار مدخل العبد في معنى هذا الاسم

### | القوي المتين

القوة تدل على القدرة التامة والمتانة تدل على شدة القوة والله سبحانه
وتعالى من حيث إنه بالغ القدرة تامها قوي ومن حيث إنه شديدة القوة متين
وذلك يرجع إلى معاني القدرة وسيأتي ذلك
chapters.anchors:
- Root: ح ق ق (ḥ-q-q)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Core meaning is "to be due, fitting, certain, established as real"; al-ḥaqq is that which is firmly established and cannot be negated.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): In theological usage, al-Ḥaqq is the Necessary Existent (wājib al-wujūd) whose reality is self-subsistent, as opposed to the impossible (mumtaniʿ) which is pure falsehood (bāṭil).
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal (ḥaqīqah) usage denotes real existence in re (fī al-aʿyān); metaphorical (majāz) usage extends to true statements (fī al-alsinah) and true cognitions (fī al-adhhān).
- Root: و ك ل (w-k-l)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To entrust, delegate, commit a matter to another; al-wakīl is the one upon whom affairs are placed.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): True tawakkul (reliance) is exclusive to God, for He alone is self-sufficient in executing what is entrusted, without need of delegation from another.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense allows partial delegation to creatures; metaphorical absolute sense (al-wakīl al-muṭlaq) applies solely to God.
- Root: ق و ي (q-w-y) and م ت ن (m-t-n)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Quwwah is power or capacity; matānah is hardness, firmness, and intensity of strength.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Quwwah in God is perfect and complete power (qudrah tāmmah); matānah intensifies this to absolute invincibility.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Both are literal attributes of God, not metaphorical, since they denote His essential perfection.
- Sībawayh Rule: Rule of Taqābūl (Contrastive Definition) — "al-ashyāʾ qad tustabānu bi-aḍdādihā" (things are made clear by their opposites); also Rule of Istiḥqāq bi-al-Dhāt (Self-Desert) — distinguishing what is deserved by essence versus by another, parsed through the particle "min ḥaythu" (in respect of) to mark aspectual predication.
chapters.translation:
### | The Truth (al-Ḥaqq)

It is the opposite of falsehood (al-bāṭil), and things are often made clear by their opposites. Everything of which one speaks is either absolutely false, or absolutely true, or true in one respect and false in another. That which is impossible in itself (al-mumtaniʿ bi-dhātihi) is absolutely false; that which is necessary in itself (al-wājib bi-dhātihi) is absolutely true; and that which is possible in itself but necessary through another (al-mumkin bi-dhātihi al-wājib bi-ghayrihi) is true in one respect and false in another. For in respect of its own essence, it has no existence, so it is false; and in respect of another, it acquires existence, so in that respect which faces the giver of existence, it is existent — thus it is true in that respect and false in respect of itself. Therefore the Exalted said: {«كُلُّ شَيْءٍ هَالِكٌ إِلَّا وَجْهَهُ»} (Everything is perishing except His Face) — Surah al-Qaṣaṣ 28:88. And this is so eternally and perpetually, not in one state rather than another, because everything other than Him, eternally and perpetually, in respect of its own essence does not deserve existence, and in respect of Him it deserves it. So it is false in itself, true through another. And by this you come to know that the absolutely True (al-Ḥaqq al-muṭlaq) is the truly Existent in Himself, from whom every truth takes its reality.

It is also said of the intelligible (al-maʿqūl) which the intellect encounters as matching the existent until it corresponds to it, that it is true. So in respect of its own essence it is called "existent," and in respect of its relation to the intellect that apprehends it as it is, it is called "true." Thus the most deserving of existents to be true is God — exalted be He — and the most deserving of cognitions to be true is knowledge of God, mighty and majestic. For He is true in Himself, i.e., corresponding to the known, eternally and perpetually; and His correspondence is to His own essence, not to another — unlike knowledge of the existence of another, which is only true as long as that other exists; when it ceases, that belief reverts to falsehood. And that belief also is not true for the sake of the believer's essence, because he is not existent in himself but existent through another.

This term is also applied to statements, and one says "a true saying" and "a false saying." On that basis, the truest of statements is your saying: "There is no god but God" (lā ilāha illā Allāh), because it is truthful eternally and perpetually, in itself, not through another.

Thus "truth" is applied to existence in external things (al-aʿyān), to existence in minds (al-adhhān) which is cognition, and to existence on the tongue (al-lisān) which is utterance. So the most deserving of things to be true is that whose existence is established in itself, eternally and perpetually; whose cognition is true eternally and perpetually; and whose attestation is true eternally and perpetually — and all of that is for the sake of the truly Existent Himself, not for another.

**Admonition (tanbīh):** The servant's share of this name is that he see himself as false (bāṭil) and see nothing other than God, mighty and majestic, as true. And if the servant is true, he is not true in himself but true through God, mighty and majestic — for he exists through Him, not through himself; rather, in himself he is false, were it not for the True's bringing him into existence. So he who says "I am the Truth" (anā al-ḥaqq) has erred, except under one of two interpretations:

The first is that he means "I am through the Truth" — but this interpretation is remote, because the wording does not indicate it, and because it does not single him out, since everything other than the Truth is through the Truth.

The second interpretation is that he is so overwhelmed by the Truth that there is no room in him for anything else; and when a thing takes hold of a thing entirely and overwhelms it, it may be said that it is it — as the poet says:

"I am the one I love, and the one I love is I — we are two spirits dwelling in one body."

And he means thereby total absorption (al-istighrāq).

Now, because the Sufis (ahl al-taṣawwuf) are dominated by the vision of the annihilation of their own selves in respect of their essence, the name of God most frequently on their tongues — in most of their sayings and states — is "the Truth" (al-Ḥaqq), for they behold the true Essence rather than that which is perishing in itself.

And because the theologians (ahl al-kalām) are more remote, standing at the station of inference from acts, the name most frequently on their tongues is "the Originator" (al-Bāriʾ), which carries the meaning of "the Creator" (al-Khāliq).

And most of creation see everything other than Him, so they bear witness to Him by what they see — and they are the ones addressed by His saying, the Exalted: {«أَوَلَمْ يَنْظُرُوا فِي مَلَكُوتِ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَمَا خَلَقَ اللَّهُ مِنْ شَيْءٍ»} (Have they not looked upon the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and what God has created of all things?) — Surah al-Aʿrāf 7:185.

But the veracious ones (al-ṣiddīqūn) see nothing other than Him, so they bear witness to Him by Him — and they are the ones addressed by His saying, the Exalted: {«أَوَلَمْ يَكْفِ بِرَبِّكَ أَنَّهُ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ شَهِيدٌ»} (Is it not sufficient that your Lord is, over all things, a Witness?) — Surah Fuṣṣilat 41:53.

### | The Trustee (al-Wakīl)

He is the one to whom affairs are entrusted. But the one entrusted is divided into: one to whom some affairs are entrusted — and that is deficient; and one to whom everything is entrusted — and that is none other than God, glorified and exalted. And the one entrusted is also divided into: one who deserves to be entrusted not in himself but by delegation and appointment — and this is deficient, because he is in need of the delegation and appointment; and one who deserves in himself that affairs be entrusted to him and hearts rely upon him, without appointment or delegation from another — and that is the absolute Trustee (al-wakīl al-muṭlaq). The trustee is also divided into: one who fulfills what is entrusted to him with complete fulfillment, without shortcoming; and one who does not fulfill it all. The absolute Trustee is the one to whom affairs are entrusted, who is fully capable of undertaking them and fulfills their completion — and that is God alone, exalted be He. And from this you have understood the extent of the servant's entry into the meaning of this name.

### | The Strong (al-Qawī), The Firm (al-Matīn)

"Strength" (al-quwwah) indicates perfect power (al-qudrah al-tāmmah), and "firmness" (al-matānah) indicates the intensity of strength. God, glorified and exalted, is "Strong" in that He is complete and perfect in power, and "Firm" in that His strength is intense. And this reverts to the meanings of power (al-qudrah), which will come later.

chapters.arabic_text:
### | الولي

هو المحب الناصر ومعنى وده ومحبته قد سبق ومعنى نصرته ظاهر فإنه يقمع
أعداء الدين وينصر أولياءه قال الله سبحانه وتعالى الله ولي الذين آمنوا
وقال تعالى ذلك بأن الله مولى الذين آمنوا وأن الكافرين لا مولى لهم
محمد الآية 11 أي لا ناصر لهم وقال عز وجل كتب الله لأغلبن أنا ورسلي 58
سورة المجادلة الآية 21 تنبيه
الولي من العباد من يحب الله عز وجل ويحب أولياءه وينصره وينصر أولياءه
ويعادي أعداءه ومن أعدائه النفس والشيطان فمن خذلهما ونصر أمر الله تعالى
ووالى أولياء الله وعادى أعداءه فهو الولي من العباد

### | الحميد

هو المحمود المثنى عليه والله عز وجل هو الحميد بحمده لنفسه أزلا وبحمد
عباده له أبدا ويرجع هذا إلى صفات الجلال والعلو والكمال منسوبا إلى ذكر
الذاكرين له فإن الحمد هو ذكر أوصاف الكمال من حيث هو كمال تنبيه
الحميد من العباد من حمدت عقائده وأخلاقه وأعماله وأقواله كلها من غير
مثنوية وذاك هو محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم ومن يقرب منه من الأنبياء ومن
عداهم من الأولياء والعلماء وكل واحد منهم حميد بقدر ما  يحمد من عقائده
وأخلاقه وأعماله وأقواله وإذا كان لا يخلو أحد عن مذمة ونقص وإن كثرت
محامده فالحميد المطلق هو الله تعالى

### | المحصي

هو العالم ولكن إذا أضيف العلم إلى المعلومات من حيث يحصي
المعلومات ويعدها ويحيط بها سمي إحصاء والمحصي المطلق هو الذي ينكشف في
علمه حد كل معلوم وعدده ومبلغه
والعبد وإن أمكنه أن يحصي بعلمه بعض المعلومات فإنه يعجز عن حصر أكثرها
فمدخله في هذا الاسم ضعيف كمدخله في أصل العلم

### | المبدئ المعيد

معناه الموجد لكن الإيجاد إذا لم يكن مسبوقا بمثله سمي إبداء وإذا كان
مسبوقا بمثله سمي إعادة والله سبحانه وتعالى بدأ خلق الناس ثم هو الذي
يعيدهم أي يحشرهم والأشياء كلها منه بدأت وإليه تعود وبه بدأت وبه تعود

### | المحيي المميت

هذا أيضا يرجع إلى الإيجاد ولكن الموجود إذ كان هو الحياة سمي فعله إحياء
وإذا كان هو الموت سمي فعله إماتة ولا خالق للموت و

### | الحي

اة إلا الله سبحانه وتعالى فلا مميت ولا محيي إلا الله عز وجل وقد سبقت
الإشارة إلى معنى الحياة في اسم الباعث فلا نعيده
الحي
هو الفعال الدراك حتى إن من لا فعل له أصلا ولا إدراك فهو ميت وأقل درجات
الإدراك أن يشعر المدرك بنفسه فما لا يشعر بنفسه فهو الجماد والميت فالحي
الكامل المطلق هو الذي يندرج جميع المدركات تحت إدراكه وجميع الموجودات تحت
فعله حتى لا يشذ عن علمه مدرك ولا عن فعله مفعول وذلك الله عز وجل فهو الحي
المطلق وكل حي سواه
فحياته بقدر إدراكه وفعله وكل ذلك محصور في قلة ثم إن الأحياء يتفاوتون
فيه فمراتبهم بقدر تفاوتهم كما سبقت الإشارة إليه في مراتب الملائكة والإنس
والبهائم

### | القيوم

اعلم أن الأشياء تنقسم إلى ما يفتقر إلى محل كالأغراض والأوصاف فيقال
فيها إنها ليست قائمة بأنفسها وإلى ما يحتاج إلى محل فيقال إنه قائم بنفسه
كالجواهر إلا أن الجوهر وإن قام بنفسه مستغنيا عن محل يقوم به فليس مستغنيا
عن أمور لا  بد منها لوجوده وتكون شرطا في وجوده فلا يكون قائما بنفسه لأنه
يحتاج في قوامه إلى وجود غيره وإن لم يحتج إلى محل
فإن كان في الوجود موجود يكفي ذاته بذاته ولا قوام له بغيره ولا يشترط في
دوام وجوده وجود غيره فهو القائم بنفسه مطلقا فإن كان مع ذلك يقوم به كل
موجود حتى لا يتصور للأشياء وجود ولا دوام وجود إلا به فهو القيوم لأن
قوامه بذاته وقوام كل شيء به وليس ذلك إلا الله سبحانه وتعالى
ومدخل العبد في هذا الوصف بقدر استغنائه عما سوى الله تعالى

### | الواجد

هو الذي لا يعوزه شيء وهو في مقابلة الفاقد ولعل من فاته ما لا حاجة به
إلى وجوده لا يسمى فاقدا والذي يحضره ما لا تعلق له بذاته ولا بكمال ذاته
لا يسمى واجدا بل الواجد من لا يعوزه شيء مما لا بد منه وكل ما لا بد منه
في صفات الإلهية وكمالها فهو موجود لله سبحانه وتعالى فهو بهذا
الاعتبار واجد وهو الواجد المطلق ومن عداه إن كان واجدا لشيء من صفات
الكمال وأسبابه فهو فاقد لأشياء فلا يكون واجدا إلا بالإضافة

### | الماجد

بمعنى المجيد كالعالم بمعنى العليم لكن الفعيل أكثر مبالغة وقد سبق معناه
chapters.anchors:
- Root: و-ل-ي (w-l-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Proximity, guardianship, and assuming command over a matter; the walī is the one who is near and takes charge.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): The walī is the one who aids and befriends; God's wilāyah denotes His governance and protection of the believer.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal sense of closeness and management; metaphorically extended to love and succor.
- Root: ح-م-د (ḥ-m-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To praise, commend, or extol; opposite of dhamm (blame).
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ḥamd is the mention of attributes of perfection, whether in gratitude or pure laudation.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal praise of virtue; metaphorical when applied to God as eternal self-praise.
- Root: ح-ص-ي (ḥ-ṣ-y)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To count, enumerate, or encompass numerically.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Iḥṣāʾ is comprehensive knowledge of the particulars and limits of all things.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal counting; metaphorical for exhaustive divine knowledge.
- Root: ب-د-أ (b-d-ʾ) and ع-و-د (ʿ-w-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Ibdāʾ is origination without precedent; iʿādah is bringing back after annihilation.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Ibdāʾ is creation ex nihilo; iʿādah is the second creation at resurrection.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for temporal beginnings; metaphorical for divine re-creation.
- Root: ح-ي-ي (ḥ-y-y) and م-و-ت (m-w-t)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Life is the opposite of death; iḥyāʾ is granting life, imātah is causing death.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Life is the power of perception and action; death is its absence.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for biological life; metaphorical for spiritual vitality.
- Root: ق-و-م (q-w-m)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To stand, subsist, or uphold; qiyām is self-standing.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Al-Qayyūm is He who subsists by Himself and by whom all things subsist.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal standing; metaphorical for self-sufficiency and sustaining all existence.
- Root: و-ج-د (w-j-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To find, possess, or lack nothing; wujūd is existence or finding.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Al-Wājid is He who lacks nothing needful for His essence or perfection.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal finding; metaphorical for absolute sufficiency.
- Root: م-ج-د (m-j-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Glory, honor, and nobility; majīd is the one of abundant glory.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Majd is the perfection of noble attributes.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for honor; synonymous with ḥamd in intensity.
- Sībawayh Rule: Nominal Sentences with Predicate Emphasis (al-Mubtadaʾ wa al-Khabar) — The pattern "Allah is..." (e.g., «الله ولي الذين آمنوا») uses a definite predicate to assert essential, permanent attributes, not accidental states.
chapters.translation:
### | The Guardian (al-Walī)

He is the Loving Helper. The meaning of His love (wudd) and His affection (maḥabbah) has already preceded, and the meaning of His help (nuṣrah) is apparent, for He crushes the enemies of religion and aids His friends. God, exalted and majestic, said: {«الله ولي الذين آمنوا»} "God is the Guardian of those who believe." And He, exalted, said: {«ذلك بأن الله مولى الذين آمنوا وأن الكافرين لا مولى لهم»} "That is because God is the Protector of those who believe, and the disbelievers have no protector" (Muḥammad 47:11), meaning they have no helper. And He, mighty and majestic, said: {«كتب الله لأغلبن أنا ورسلي»} "God has written: 'I will surely prevail, I and My messengers'" (al-Mujādilah 58:21).

**Admonition:** The walī among servants is the one who loves God, mighty and majestic, and loves His friends, and helps Him and helps His friends, and takes as enemies His enemies. Among His enemies are the ego (nafs) and Satan. So whoever abandons these two, and aids the command of God, and befriends the friends of God, and opposes His enemies — he is the walī among servants.

### | The Praiseworthy (al-Ḥamīd)

He is the One praised and extolled. God, mighty and majestic, is al-Ḥamīd by His own praise of Himself eternally (azalan), and by the praise of His servants for Him everlastingly (abadan). This reverts to the attributes of majesty, exaltation, and perfection, as related to the remembrance of those who remember Him. For praise (ḥamd) is the mention of attributes of perfection, insofar as they are perfection.

**Admonition:** The ḥamīd among servants is the one whose beliefs, character, deeds, and words are all praised, without any blameworthiness. That is Muḥammad, peace be upon him, and those near to him among the prophets. Beyond them are the friends (awliyāʾ) and scholars. Each of them is praiseworthy to the extent that his beliefs, character, deeds, and words are praised. And since no one is free from blame and deficiency, however numerous his praiseworthy qualities, the absolutely Praiseworthy (al-Ḥamīd al-Muṭlaq) is God, exalted.

### | The Reckoner (al-Muḥṣī)

He is the Knower (al-ʿĀlim), but when knowledge is related to known things insofar as He enumerates them, counts them, and encompasses them, it is called enumeration (iḥṣāʾ). The absolutely Reckoning One is He in whose knowledge the limit, number, and extent of every known thing is disclosed.

As for the servant, even if he can enumerate some known things by his knowledge, he is incapable of encompassing most of them. So his entry into this name is weak, like his entry into the root of knowledge itself.

### | The Originator and Restorer (al-Mubdiʾ al-Muʿīd)

Its meaning is the Existentiator (al-Mūjid). But origination (ījād), when not preceded by its like, is called initiation (ibdāʾ); and when preceded by its like, it is called restoration (iʿādah). God, glorified and exalted, initiated the creation of mankind, then He is the One who restores them — that is, He gathers them. All things from Him began, and to Him they return; by Him they began, and by Him they return.

### | The Life-Giver and Death-Giver (al-Muḥyī al-Mumīt)

This too reverts to existentiation (ījād). But when the existent is life itself, His act is called giving life (iḥyāʾ); and when it is death itself, His act is called giving death (imātah). There is no creator of death and life except God, glorified and exalted. So there is no death-giver and no life-giver except God, mighty and majestic. The indication of the meaning of life has already preceded in the name "The Resurrector" (al-Bāʿith), so we shall not repeat it.

### | The Living (al-Ḥayy)

He is the Agent (al-Faʿʿāl) and the Perceiver (al-Darrāk). Indeed, whoever has no act at all and no perception is dead. The lowest degree of perception is that the perceiver is aware of himself. So whatever is not aware of itself is the inanimate (al-jamād) and the dead. The complete, absolute Living One is He under whose perception all perceived things fall, and under whose act all existent things fall, so that no perceived thing escapes His knowledge, and no effected thing escapes His act. That is God, mighty and majestic. He is the absolutely Living. Every living being other than Him — its life is proportionate to its perception and act, and all of that is confined to scarcity. Then the living beings differ in this, so their ranks are proportionate to their difference, as was indicated in the ranks of angels, humans, and beasts.

### | The Self-Subsisting (al-Qayyūm)

Know that things divide into what needs a substrate (maḥall), like accidents (aʿrāḍ) and attributes — these are said not to subsist by themselves — and into what needs no substrate, which is said to subsist by itself, like substances (jawāhir). However, the substance, though it subsists by itself independent of a substrate, is not independent of things indispensable for its existence, which are conditions for its existence. So it is not self-subsisting, because it needs the existence of another for its subsistence, even if it does not need a substrate.

If there exists in existence a being whose essence suffices for itself, with no subsistence through another, and no existence of another is a condition for the perpetuity of its existence, then it is the absolutely Self-Subsisting (al-Qāʾim bi-Nafsihi Muṭlaqan). If, moreover, every existent subsists through it, so that no existence or perpetuity of existence is conceivable for things except through it, then it is al-Qayyūm — because its subsistence is through itself, and the subsistence of everything is through it. That is none other than God, glorified and exalted.

The servant's entry into this description is proportionate to his independence from all other than God, exalted.

### | The Self-Sufficient Finder (al-Wājid)

He is the One for whom nothing is lacking. It is the opposite of the deprived (al-fāqid). Perhaps one who misses what he has no need for is not called deprived; and one who possesses what has no relation to his essence or the perfection of his essence is not called a finder. Rather, the wājid is the one for whom nothing indispensable is lacking. Everything indispensable for the attributes of divinity and their perfection is present for God, glorified and exalted. So by this consideration, He is wājid — He is the absolutely Wājid. As for anyone other than Him, if he is a finder of some attributes of perfection and their causes, he is deprived of other things. So he is not wājid except relatively.

### | The Glorious (al-Mājid)

It is synonymous with al-Majīd, just as al-ʿĀlim is synonymous with al-ʿAlīm. But the form faʿīl is more intensive in exaggeration. Its meaning has already preceded.

chapters.title_en: The One, The Self-Sufficient, The Powerful, The Omnipotent, The Advancer, The Deferrer, The First, The Last
chapters.arabic_text:
### | الواحد

هو الذي لا يتجرأ ولا يثنى
أما الذي لا يتجزأ فكالجوهر الواحد الذي لا ينقسم فيقال إنه واحد بمعنى
أنه لا جزء له وكذا النقطة لا جزء لها والله تعالى واحد بمعنى أنه يستحيل
تقدير الانقسام في ذاته
وأما الذي لا يتثنى فهو الذي لا نظير له كالشمس مثلا فإنها وإن كانت
قابلة للانقسام بالوهم متجزئة في ذاتها لأنها من قبيل الأجسام فهي لا نظير
لها إلا أنه يمكن أن يكون لها نظير فإن كان في الوجود موجود يتفرد بخصوص
وجوده تفردا لا يتصور أن يشاركه غيره فيه أصلا فهو الواحد المطلق أزلا
وأبدا
والعبد إنما يكون واحدا إذا لم يكن له في أبناء جنسه نظير في خصلة من
خصال الخير وذلك  بالإضافة إلى أبناء جنسه وبالإضافة إلى الوقت إذ يمكن أن
يظهر في وقت آخر مثله وبالإضافة إلى بعض الخصال دون الجميع فلا وحدة على
الإطلاق إلا لله تعالى

### | الصمد

هو الذي يصمد إليه في الحوائج ويقصد إليه في الرغائب إذ ينتهي إليه منتهى
السؤدد ومن جعله الله تعالى مقصد عباده في مهمات دينهم ودنياهم وأجرى على
يده ولسانه حوائج خلقه فقد أنعم عليه بحظ من معنى هذا الوصف لكن الصمد
المطلق هو الذي يقصد إليه في جميع الحوائج وهو الله سبحانه وتعالى

### | القادر المقتدر

معناهما ذو القدرة لكن المقتدر أكثر مبالغة والقدرة عبارة عن المعنى الذي
به يوجد الشيء متقدرا بتقدير الإرادة والعلم واقعا على وفقهما والقادر هو
الذي إن شاء فعل وإن شاء لم يفعل وليس من شرطه أن يشاء لا محالة فإن الله
قادر على إقامة القيامة الآن لأنه لو شاء أقامها فإن كان لا يقيمها لأنه لم
يشأها ولا يشاؤها لما جرى في سابق علمه من تقدير أجلها ووقتها فلذلك لا
يقدح في القدرة والقادر المطلق هو الذي يخترع كل موجود اختراعا يتفرد به
ويستغني فيه عن معاونة غيره وهو الله تعالى
وأما العبد فله قدرة على الجملة ولكنها ناقصة إذ لا يتناول إلا بعض
الممكنات ولا يصلح للاختراع بل الله تعالى هو المخترع لمقدورات العبد
بواسطة قدرته مهما هيأ له جميع أسباب الوجود لمقدوره وتحت هذا غور لا يحتمل
مثل هذا الكتاب كشفه

### | المقدم والمؤخر

هو الذي يقرب ويبعد ومن قربه فقد قدمه ومن أبعده فقد أخره وقد قدم
أنبياءه وأولياءه بتقريبهم وهدايتهم وأخر أعداءه بإبعادهم وضرب الحجاب بينه
وبينهم والملك إذا قرب شخصين مثلا ولكن جعل أحدهما أقرب إلى نفسه يقال قدمه
أي جعله قدام غيره
والقدام تارة يكون في المكان وتارة يكون في الرتبة وهو مضاف لا محالة إلى
متأخر عنه ولا بد فيه من مقصد هو الغاية بالإضافة إليه يتقدم ما يتقدم
ويتأخر ما يتأخر والمقصد هو الله سبحانه وتعالى والمقدم عند الله  تعالى هو
المقرب فقد قدم الملائكة ثم الأنبياء ثم الأولياء ثم العلماء وكل متأخر فهو
مؤخر بالإضافة إلى ما قبله مقدم بالإضافة إلى ما بعده والله سبحانه وتعالى
هو المقدم والمؤخر لأنك إذا أحلت تقدمهم وتأخرهم على توفيرهم وتقصيرهم
وكمالهم في الصفات ونقصهم فمن الذي حملهم على التوفير بالعلم والعبادة
بإثارة دواعيهم ومن الذي حملهم على التقصير بصرف دواعيهم إلى ضد الصراط
المستقيم وذلك كله من الله تعالى فهو المقدم والمؤخر والمراد هو التقديم
والتأخير في الرتبة وفيه إشارة إلى أنه لم يتقدم من تقدم بعلمه وعمله بل
بتقديم الله عز وجل إياه وكذلك المتأخر وقد صرح بذلك قوله تعالى إن الذين
سبقت لهم منا الحسنى أولئك عنها مبعدون 21 سورة الأنبياء الآية 101 وقوله
تعالى ولو شئنا لآتينا كل نفس هداها ولكن حق القول مني لأملأن جهنم 32 سورة
السجدة الآية 13 تنبيه
حظ العبد من صفات الأفعال ظاهر فلذلك قد لا نشتغل بإعادته في كل اسم حذرا
من التطويل إذ فيما ذكرناه تعريف لطريق الكلام

### | الأول والآخر

اعلم أن الأول يكون أولا بالإضافة إلى شيء والآخر يكون آخرا بالإضافة إلى
شيء وهما متناقضان فلا يتصور أن يكون الشيء الواحد من وجه واحد بالإضافة
إلى شيء واحد أولا وآخرا جميعا بل إذا نظرت إلى
ترتيب الوجود ولاحظت سلسلة الموجودات المترتبة فالله تعالى بالإضافة
إليها أول إذ الموجودات كلها استفادت الوجود منه وأما هو فموجود بذاته وما
استفاد الوجود من غيره
ومهما نظرت إلى ترتيب السلوك ولاحظت مراتب منازل السائرين إليه فهو آخر
إذ هو آخر ما يرتقي إليه درجات العارفين وكل معرفة تحصل قبل معرفته فهي
مرقاة إلى معرفته والمنزل الأقصى هو معرفة الله سبحانه وتعالى فهو آخر
بالإضافة إلى السلوك أول بالإضافة إلى الوجود فمنه المبدأ أولا وإليه
المرجع والمصير آخرا
chapters.anchors:
- Root: و-ح-د (w-ḥ-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Singularity, oneness; that which has no second or peer; indivisibility in essence or attribute.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Al-Wāḥid denotes absolute uniqueness in essence and attributes, exclusive to God; for creatures, unity is relative and contingent.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for God (Ḥaqīqah) — indivisible and peerless; metaphorical (Majāz) for creatures — unity by comparison to peers in specific traits.
- Root: ص-م-د (ṣ-m-d)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: To direct oneself toward someone for needs; the master whose authority is final; that which is solid, without hollow interior.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Al-Ṣamad is the one to whom all creatures turn for every need, ultimate in sovereignty and refuge.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for God — absolute terminus of all petitions; metaphorical for creatures — partial share in being sought for some needs.
- Root: ق-د-ر (q-d-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Measure, capacity, power to bring about existence in accordance with will and knowledge.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Al-Qādir is one who acts or refrains by will; al-Muqtadir intensifies this — absolute origination without aid.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for God — unrestricted power; metaphorical for the servant — limited capacity over some possibles, not origination.
- Root: ق-د-م (q-d-m) and أ-خ-ر (a-kh-r)
  * Lisān / ʿAyn: Q-d-m: precedence, proximity; a-kh-r: delay, distance. Both relational terms requiring a reference point.
  * Al-Rāghib (Mufradāt): Divine precedence is by rank and proximity to God, not by time; divine deferral is by distance from Him.
  * Al-Zamakhsharī (Asās): Literal for spatial/temporal order; metaphorical for spiritual rank — God's advancing and deferring are acts of will.
- Sībawayh Rule: Al-Idāfah al-Maʿnawiyyah (Construct state conveying relational meaning) — terms like "first" and "last" are inherently relational (muḍāf), requiring a terminus (muḍāf ilayh) to complete their sense; the absolute terminus is God Himself.
chapters.translation:
### | The One (al-Wāḥid)

He is the one who is neither divisible nor has a second.

As for that which is not divisible — like the single atom (al-jawhar al-wāḥid) that does not divide, so it is said to be "one" meaning it has no part; likewise the point has no part. God, exalted, is "One" in the sense that it is impossible to conceive division in His essence.

As for that which has no second — it is that which has no peer, like the sun, for example. For although it is divisible in imagination and partitioned in its essence (since it belongs to the class of bodies), it has no peer — yet it is possible that a peer could exist for it. But if there exists in existence a being that is unique in the particularity of its existence, in a uniqueness such that it is inconceivable that any other could share in it at all, then that is the absolutely One, eternally and everlastingly.

The servant is only "one" when he has no peer among his fellow kind in some trait of the traits of goodness — and that is relative to his fellow kind, and relative to the time (for it is possible that another like him might appear at another time), and relative to some traits rather than all. So there is no absolute unity except for God, exalted.

### | The Self-Sufficient (al-Ṣamad)

He is the one to whom one directs oneself in needs and toward whom one turns in desires, for to Him terminates the utmost of sovereignty. And whoever God, exalted, makes the object of His servants' seeking in the important matters of their religion and their worldly life, and runs upon his hand and tongue the needs of His creatures — He has bestowed upon him a share of the meaning of this attribute. But the absolutely Self-Sufficient is the one toward whom all needs are directed, and He is God, glorified and exalted.

### | The Powerful, The Omnipotent (al-Qādir, al-Muqtadir)

Their meaning is "possessor of power" (dhū qudrah), but al-Muqtadir is more intensive in degree. Power (al-qudrah) is an expression for the attribute by which a thing comes to exist measured by the measure of will and knowledge, occurring in accordance with them both. And the Powerful (al-Qādir) is the one who, if He wills, acts, and if He wills, does not act. It is not a condition of His power that He must will necessarily. For God is powerful over establishing the Hour now, because if He willed, He would establish it. If He does not establish it, it is because He has not willed it — and He does not will it because of what has preceded in His eternal knowledge of the apportioning of its term and its time. Therefore this does not impugn power.

And the absolutely Powerful is the one who originates (yakhtariʿ) every existent with an origination in which He is unique and in which He is independent of the aid of any other — and He is God, exalted.

As for the servant, he has power in a general sense, but it is deficient, for it does not extend except to some possibles, and it is not suited for origination. Rather, God, exalted, is the originator of the servant's acts of power (maqdūrāt) by means of the servant's power, whenever He has prepared for him all the causes of existence for his act of power. Beneath this there is a depth that a book like this cannot bear to unveil.

### | The Advancer and The Deferrer (al-Muqaddim, al-Muʾakhkhir)

He is the one who brings near and who distances. Whom He brings near, He has advanced; whom He distances, He has deferred. He advanced His prophets and His saints by bringing them near and guiding them, and He deferred His enemies by distancing them and casting a veil between Him and them. When a king, for example, brings two persons near but makes one of them nearer to himself, it is said he "advanced" him — i.e., he placed him ahead of the other.

Precedence (al-taqdīm) is sometimes in place and sometimes in rank, and it is necessarily relative to something that comes after it. There must be a terminus (maqṣid) that is the goal, in relation to which what advances advances and what is deferred is deferred. And the terminus is God, glorified and exalted. The one advanced with God, exalted, is the one brought near. Thus He advanced the angels, then the prophets, then the saints, then the scholars. And every one that comes after is "deferred" relative to what precedes it and "advanced" relative to what follows it.

God, glorified and exalted, is the Advancer and the Deferrer, because when you trace their advancement and deferral back to their completeness and deficiency, and their perfection in attributes and their lack — who is it that drove them to completeness through knowledge and worship by arousing their motives, and who drove them to deficiency by turning their motives toward the opposite of the straight path? All of that is from God, exalted. So He is the Advancer and the Deferrer. The intended meaning is advancement and deferral in rank. And in this there is an indication that no one advanced advanced by his own knowledge and deed, but by God's, mighty and majestic, advancing him — and likewise the one deferred. This is explicitly stated in His saying, exalted: {«إِنَّ الَّذِينَ سَبَقَتْ لَهُمْ مِنَّا الْحُسْنَىٰ أُولَٰئِكَ عَنْهَا مُبْعَدُونَ»} (Those for whom the good [decree] has preceded from Us — they are from it kept far away) — Sūrat al-Anbiyāʾ, verse 101. And His saying, exalted: {«وَلَوْ شِئْنَا لَآتَيْنَا كُلَّ نَفْسٍ هُدَاهَا وَلَٰكِنْ حَقَّ الْقَوْلُ مِنِّي لَأَمْلَأَنَّ جَهَنَّمَ»} (And had We willed, We would have given every soul its guidance, but the word from Me has taken effect: I will surely fill Hell) — Sūrat al-Sajdah, verse 13.

**A Note (Tanbīh):** The servant's share of the attributes of acts is apparent, and therefore we may not occupy ourselves with repeating it under every name, out of caution against prolixity — for in what we have mentioned there is a definition of the method of discourse.

### | The First and The Last (al-Awwal, al-Ākhir)

Know that the "first" is first relative to something, and the "last" is last relative to something, and they are two contradictories. It is inconceivable that one single thing, from one single aspect, relative to one single thing, should be both first and last together. Rather, when you look at the order of existence and observe the chain of ordered existents, God, exalted, is "First" relative to them — for all existents have derived existence from Him. As for Him, He exists by His own essence and has not derived existence from any other.

And whenever you look at the order of the spiritual journey (al-sulūk) and observe the ranks of the stations of those journeying to Him, He is "Last" — for He is the final goal to which the degrees of the knowers ascend. Every knowledge attained before knowledge of Him is a ladder to knowledge of Him, and the farthest station is knowledge of God, glorified and exalted. So He is "Last" relative to the journey, and "First" relative to existence. From Him is the beginning first, and to Him is the return and the final end last.
